[Appendix E - Conventions Used and Other Tips](#part0019.xhtml)IntroductionThis is the third book in the Do-It-Yourself Java Games series. The first book's programs were text-based so you could develop basic Java programming skills. The second book, More Do-It-Yourself Java Games, covered a wide variety of [graphical user interfaces](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_cf298a95114c3394_fdee) for [event-driven](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_6d70e22111ecd978_faf4) games. Those games created the initial window, then waited for the program [user](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f7ee8b295ae825fc_1104a) to take an action. The games in this book require the same kind of event-driven user interfaces, but add [threads](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_2a0963431d6e1d34_10ea3) to perform automated, simultaneous activities, whether the user takes an action or not.This book introduces several advanced programming techniques:

*   Use threads to [animate](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_8a92ee931e94fa83_f293) game [objects](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_71c0aa408ef2c4da_10871) and to play [audio files](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_9bd07d7c63a02f04_f33b).
*   Understand the [event dispatch thread](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_812588057eecf796_faa6) used by Java's graphical user interface.
*   Use advanced Java types: [abstract classes](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_43e3f7b067e9b9fb_f1a9) and interfaces.
*   Use [state-driven programming](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_63ffef12e17d466c_10c86) to manage all the game activity.
*   Separate the user interface from the program logic by using [model/view/controller](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_4df0674422c946cc_106c8) design.

The games in this book will also serve as a great foundation for many other games. Once you complete a project, feel free to modify it to create other games. Half the fun of programming is making programs do what you want them to do.As in the previous books in this series, the lessons in each project are presented using a “try-it” approach: do the steps shown and see what happens. You'll be given programming tasks, each followed by a program [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f) [listing](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_8f65caac9a11e926_10538). The listings have fill-in blanks to allow you to write much of the code yourself. But don't worry if you're unsure of how to fill in the blanks; simply click the completed listing's link to see the missing code.Don't skip any lessons. Each lesson explains a new programming technique, which may be used again in later lessons. Doing all the lessons will make later lessons easier.[Appendix A - Glossary](#part0015.xhtml) has definitions of Java programming terms and links to more information. The first use of each term, like “graphical user interfaces” and “event-driven” used above, will include a [clickable](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_6414c477fad92f99_f5d8) link to the word in the glossary.The Do-It-Yourself Java Games books are designed for e-readers. Click the image below or follow this [link](http://youtu.be/XMuXNyyk7mg) to watch a video showing the features in these electronic books that would not be possible in a print book.[![](OEBPS/images/advanceddoityourselfjavagames_html_5215c330.jpg)](http://youtu.be/XMuXNyyk7mg)  The ProgramsYou'll create eight computer programs that use Java threads:My Timer![](OEBPS/images/advanceddoityourselfjavagames_html_m2e1fabe9.jpg)Learn how to create, start, and stop a thread that continually updates the display, and how to add sound to a program.My Timer counts down the number of seconds from any start time and beeps when the timer reaches zero.Speed WordsLearn how to move objects with the mouse and how to integrate the timer created for the previous program into this program's game.![](OEBPS/images/advanceddoityourselfjavagames_html_1f0653ef.jpg)Make as many other words as possible from the letters of a random seven-letter word, in sixty seconds.Match Three![](OEBPS/images/advanceddoityourselfjavagames_html_m17ad0f59.jpg)Learn how to use a thread to automatically move objects.Swap balls to form chains of three or more matching balls. Completed chains will be removed and replaced by new balls. Score more points for longer chains.Baby BirdLearn to create continuous motion using a [Swing](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_de31657f4ed0ea83_10ddf) timer and learn to [detect collisions](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_6694df8b159b0fad_f620).![](OEBPS/images/advanceddoityourselfjavagames_html_20ef9f2f.jpg)Flap the baby bird's wings to guide the bird through the gaps in the walls. More points are given for flying through smaller gaps.Falling Bricks![](OEBPS/images/advanceddoityourselfjavagames_html_794b8c6b.jpg)Learn to use abstract classes.Move, rotate, and drop falling bricks to complete rows. Earn more points by completing multiple rows with a single brick.Gravity Well![](OEBPS/images/advanceddoityourselfjavagames_html_m478fe6ff.jpg)Learn to use state-driven programming for managing game activity and to detect collisions of irregularly-shaped objects.Softly land a spaceship without crashing into walls or using up all the fuel. The softer and the more difficult the landing pad, the more points are awarded and the more fuel is replenished.Cat and Mouse![](OEBPS/images/advanceddoityourselfjavagames_html_110422bc.jpg)Learn to use an [interface](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d74c9b6cbdca9d02_10111) for more efficient state-driven code.Guide the mouse to eat cheese without getting caught by the cat. Be careful - the cat can hear when the mouse moves and will try to hunt it down.Blitz![](OEBPS/images/advanceddoityourselfjavagames_html_m442416f5.jpg)Learn to separate the program [logic](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e7cc05551c45ca60_1054f) from user interface using a model/view/controller design.Blitz is a popular card game also known as Scat or 31\. Try to get 31 points in one suit or rap if another player might have fewer points. But beware, anyone who raps with the worst hand must pay double.Previous Programming Knowledge RequiredThis book assumes you already know how to perform the following Java programming tasks, taught in the first two books of this series. You may skip the first two books if you already know how to perform these tasks.Do-It-Yourself Java Games: An Introduction to Java Computer Programming teaches the following tasks. Instructions for how to do the tasks that are marked with an asterisk, *, are also included at the back of this book, in [Appendix D - Using Eclipse](#part0018.xhtml).

*   *Create [Java projects](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_cf63a8be27d3ec24_101b3), [packages](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_933bf66eb34c8a11_108eb), and [classes](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592).
*   *Inherit from a [superclass](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f2efb435a19e5114_10da2) ([extend](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1257f907c91f465_fb7e) another class).
*   *Add projects to the [build path](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_16ade889aa555e58_f423).
*   Create a [main()](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e7e1b0c0266556af_105af) [method](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e7e1b0c0266556af_105af) and one or more [constructors](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1deaf7ad1648b949_f78f).
*   *Save, [run](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_33acc39cc7b992b0_10ba9), and [export](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_34cba8e9160a0039_fb61) a program into an executable [JAR file](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_5d5d59d7dce4a8ac_10191).
*   [Import](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_c3e10909de23d057_ff85) other classes.
*   Create and use [variables of types](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1efec72ee65afe7_1105b): [string](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_636f36eeb6f3b8f0_10d22), [int](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_92b7614274f15d5e_100cf), [long](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_9e655349e5fdc8e3_1058a), [double](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_c1e18040e6f72b93_f98c), [float](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d9b7d8aba5a9a0c6_fc78), [char](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f60e798719fa52c1_f57b), and [boolean](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_16e20a7387b40372_f37f).
*   Create and use variable modifiers: [private](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_fba82c792e60db22_109fa), [public](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_2b5021a090ed4135_10a3d), [protected](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e15aad0bd742db76_10a29), [static](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_9407a2e934506325_10cee), and/or [final](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_bb9cd4ac30b08075_fc61).
*   Create and use [methods](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c) with or without [parameters](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_17ebea10ad901503_1092e), and with or without a [return](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e35d24884a00e0a6_10b1a) value.
*   Create and use method modifiers: private, public, protected, static.
*   Use [if/else](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d4c8c577a58feec1_fe80) statements and [switch statements](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_c6fddee256a7d5b_10e2a).
*   Use [while](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_156b62d411d1ceae_110fd) [loops](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_156b62d411d1ceae_110fd) and [for](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_bf1812ac796a1473_fd9d) [loops](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_bf1812ac796a1473_fd9d).
*   Use the [not operator](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_750e33a901c76af9_1084d), [logical AND operator](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_dd06cc650df6470a_1056e), and [logical OR operator](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_be480bb981490370_1057c).
*   Add, subtract, multiply, divide, and take the [modulus](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_bce6978c74e3cfac_10702) (remainder) of numbers.
*   Change the order of operation using parentheses.
*   Convert a string value to an [integer](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d0ddb62fa6bbd7f5_100e3) value.
*   Convert an integer or [character](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f60e798719fa52c1_f57b) value to a string value.
*   Use [try/catch blocks](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_c3929929bb8b579b_10fcd) to handle one or more [exception](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_5826432d39c38488_fb22).
*   Use different string methods.
*   Use the Random class to generate a random number.
*   Add [comments](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_5d3020a98fc37ec0_f65d).
*   Print to the output [console](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a35c40908fadebe8_f777).
*   Use [arrays](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_59e210b3f891158a_f2f3) and [ArrayLists](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_c8f44561b0ff3a18_f323).
*   Read from and write to a text file.
*   End a program using System's exit() method.
*   Locate and fix [syntax errors](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_eefe20bb92c9c34a_10e59) and run time errors.

More Do-It-Yourself Java Games: An Introduction to Java Graphics and Event-Driven Programming teaches the following tasks that you must understand for doing the lessons in this book.

*   Create a standard [window](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_185c8a7e93daf2eb_1110e) on the [event queue](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_8dd4e68ee27b3589_fb03) and [pack](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_8fdd7740897bd805_108d1) it to set its size.
*   Create a standard custom [panel](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_3b846c32aa26cc4f_10905): set the [preferred size](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e9343816b6879acf_1099e), paint the [component](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685), and [repaint](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_b370d9d07ee4e9ed_10a9c) it as needed.
*   Use [containers](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_b473cd3a3256c48c_f7a9): frames, panels, and scroll panes, and set their [serial version UID](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_eb091c16f8916ac1_10bff).
*   Use input/display components: [buttons](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a7e3bb01f1245fef_f441), [labels](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_404728b6c38127f6_1042b), and text areas.
*   Use [listeners](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1544cc5956846959_104e5): [action listeners](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_758ae1df46aac78d_f1ef), [key listeners](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e6300aa859686c17_10379), [mouse listeners](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_c0392751225e8a1b_10710) and [mouse motion listeners](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_ce582b362207f410_10734).
*   Use input [dialogs](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d50e18f9bae39dff_f933): [message dialogs](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_b78b46ccaf904d59_1062b) and [confirm dialogs](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f0afcc43f083a5b3_f760).
*   Use [layouts](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_c1ec2d706f09968d_10446): border layout, grid layout, box layout, and flow layout.
*   Work with layouts: align components.
*   Draw graphics: strings, lines, rectangles, ovals, and images.
*   Use [colors](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_9cc10cc4a245bbb3_f63b), [fonts](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d3af6dcbb29e4420_fd57), and [font metrics](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_9d4674c43d54a227_fd6f).
*   Use different image types: [BufferedImage](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_49ddcaa2c6005877_f3d2) and Image.
*   Work with images: read [JPEG](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_ed800cd78e043ee_102e0) or [PNG](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7e36a2d8094f7b57_10979) image files, and get part of an image.
*   Set the [look and feel](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_5c2c632906a71978_1059e) of the program to the cross-platform look and feel.
*   Put data files into the exported JAR file.

SetupSee [Appendix C - Setup](#part0017.xhtml) if you don't have the free Java Development Kit (JDK) or an interactive development environment (IDE) set up, or if you need instructions for how to set up a Java [work folder](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d369e31cd16388b4_111fc). You may use any IDE, but this book's instructions refer to the free Eclipse IDE.See [Appendix D - Using Eclipse](#part0018.xhtml) if you need instructions for how to create a program using Eclipse.[Appendix E - Conventions Used and Other Tips](#part0019.xhtml) includes tips for how to use this book.Download AdvancedDIYJava.zipA variety of image and data files will be required to create the programs in this book.

1.  Download AdvancedDIYJava.zip for free from [http://www.godtlandsoftware.com/DIYJava/](http://www.godtlandsoftware.com/DIYJava/).
2.  [Extract](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_3bee7fb4fedb657e_fb9e) the files from AdvancedDIYJava.zip into your Java work folder.

See [Appendix C - Setup](#part0017.xhtml) if you need more detailed instructions for how to download AdvancedDIYJava.zip.Create the TitleLabelThe programs in this book use the same TitleLabel class that was created in one of the projects in the More Do-It-Yourself Java Games book. If you have that class, you may skip the rest of this setup and go to the first project: [Project 1 - My Timer](#part0006.xhtml).To create the TitleLabel class, do the steps in this list.

1.  Create a new Java project named My Components. (Hint: to create a project in Eclipse, right click in the Project Explorer and choose New / Java Project. Hint: the minimum JRE required for the programs in this book is Java SE 1.8\. When you create the project, select a JRE of Java SE 1.8 or higher.)
2.  Create a new package named ___________._____________.mycomponents in the project. (Hint: to create a package in Eclipse, right click on the project and choose New / Package. Hint: fill in the blanks with a unique package name. As explained in the first book, the package name should be unique to you, all lowercase, no spaces, and names separated by periods. Most businesses use their company name. You could use your first and last name. I'll use annette.godtland throughout these examples.)
3.  Create in the mycomponents package a new class named TitleLabel, which uses [JLabel](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_4a3a569a571bde6d_10257) as its superclass and has no [stub](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_53dcacfbfe94db1f_10d59) code. (Hint: to create a class in Eclipse, right click on the package and choose New / Class. Hint: the only modifier needed is public. Hint: to easily enter the superclass, click Browse..., start typing the name of the superclass, then select the superclass from the list. Hint: when not specified as right click, click means to click on the object using the left mouse button.)
    1.  Use [Quick Fix](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_53a2845c480e6047_10a6b) to add a private static final long integer variable named serialVersionUID, set to 1L. Remove the comments added with serialVersionUID. (Hint: rest the cursor on TitleLabel, which is marked as a warning, wait for the quick fix choices to appear, then select Add default serial version UID.)
    2.  Add a TitleLabel constructor coded exactly as shown. The code will set the font, color, opacity, alignment, and text of the label. (Hint: import Font and Color from java.awt.)

Listing 0-1, from TitleLabel.java

* * *

package annette.godtland.mycomponents;

import java.awt.Color;
import java.awt.Font;

import javax.swing.JLabel;

public class TitleLabel extends JLabel {
  private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;

  public TitleLabel(String title) {
    Font font = new Font(Font.SERIF, Font.BOLD, 32);
    setFont(font);
    setBackground(Color.BLACK);
    setForeground(Color.WHITE);
    setOpaque(true);
    setHorizontalAlignment(JLabel.CENTER);
    setText(title);
  }
}

*   Create each program in its own project. Form the project name using standard title capitalization with spaces between words.

[Completed listing](#part0016_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_c418b163359b5750_112ea)Run ItThe window should now show 00:00:00 below the title.Key Points and More

*   The main activity panel for each program in this book is a custom panel that extends JPanel and uses 1L as its serial version unique ID.
    *   Create a public static final long integer variable named serialVersionUID to prevent the compiler warning “The serializable class xxx does not declare a static final serialVersionUID field of type long”. That warning is otherwise generated for all JFrame and JPanel objects. The programs in this book never serialize the JFrame or JPanel objects, so serialVersionUID is never used and any value may be given to this variable. You could ignore this warning. However, as described in the book, More Do-It-Yourself Java Games, this book will set serialVersionUID to a value to indicate the version of the program. For the first version of these programs, use 1L as the serial version unique ID.
*   The custom panel must [override](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_9b1d97d1ea3454c_10899) JPanel's paintComponent() method. The method takes one parameter—a Graphics object—and returns nothing.
    *   Replace the functionality of a superclass's method by creating a method with the same name, parameters, return type, and modifiers. This action is referred to as overriding the method.
*   If the new paintComponent() method does not paint the entire [background](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_2bc944fb82244a4e_f35a) of the component, paintComponent() should call the superclass's paintComponent() method as its first line of code. For example, to call the superclass's paintComponent() method:

super.paintComponent();

*   *   A super call to an overridden method must always be the first line of code in the overriding method.
*   The Java graphics system places coordinates 0, 0 in the upper left corner of the component. Increase the coordinate values to refer to locations to the right and down from the upper left corner of the component. For example, to draw the string “Hello World” in the bottom left corner of a panel that is 100 pixels tall and whose Graphics object is named g, use:

g.drawString("Hello World", 0, 100);

*   *   To draw a string, use the coordinates for the placement of the baseline of the text. The baseline of text is the imaginary line on which the line of text rests. Some characters, such as “g” or “p” extend below the base line.
    *   To draw an image, use the coordinates for the placement of the upper left corner of the image.
*   The custom panel must override JPanel's getPreferredSize() method. The method takes no parameters and returns a Dimension object. The returned Dimension object should be the preferred size for the component when the panel's container is packed or [revalidated](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_343d27f0427d700f_10b3a).

[Completed listing](#part0016_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_3541bfda4649ee55_11325)Run ItThe window should now show 10 seconds in the new font.Key Points and More

*   Division (/) of two integers returns only the integer portion of the result. Modulo (%) of the same two integers returns only the remainder of their division. For example, 36 divided by 10 is 3 with a remainder of 6\. So 36 / 10 = 3 and 36 % 10 = 6.
*   Use String's format() method to format a string. The first parameter is the string format with text and placeholders for where to insert variable values. The remaining parameters are the variables whose values will replace the placeholders.
    *   This program used a string format with three place holders, "%02d:%02d:%02d".
    *   Placeholders all start with a percent sign (%).
    *   %d is the placeholder for a decimal integer.
    *   %2d means to reserve at least two spaces for the decimal integer.
    *   %02d means to reserve at least two spaces for the decimal integer and fill the space on the left with 0's if the integer doesn't fill the two spaces.
    *   Everything in the format string not preceded by a percent sign should be inserted between the values exactly as shown in the string. Therefore the colons (:) in the format string should be inserted between each decimal integer.
    *   To read more about how to use String's format() method to format numeric data into a string, see the Java tutorial at [http://www/docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/data/numberformat.html](http://www/docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/data/numberformat.html).

Lesson 1.4 - Pause a ThreadAll code runs in threads. Each line of code in a thread runs as soon as the previous line of code completes its task. To pause between lines of code, put the thread to sleep. However, problems may arise if you put a thread to sleep that shouldn't be put to sleep.To help you better understand how threads work, the first couple examples are common misuses of threads and demonstrate how not to put a thread to sleep.Try It - Start the TimerGo back to TimerPanel.

1.  Add a public method named start(). It should take no parameters and return nothing.

        3.  For now, print time to the console so you can see when time is updated. (Hint: use System.out's println() method.)
    2.  Call timesUp(), passing no arguments.

*   Pause the current thread using Thread's static sleep() method and the number of milliseconds to sleep.
*   sleep() must be wrapped in a try/catch block since the method may throw an interruptionException before the sleep time completes.
    *   For example, TimerPanel called return to interrupt the while loop if an interruptionException was caught.
*   Be aware that putting a thread to sleep pauses all code that was meant to run in that thread.
*   Any thread that updates windows or allows user interaction should not be paused. Code that pauses a thread should be placed on a different thread.
    *   Problems demonstrated in this lesson are typical problems seen when the thread that manages the window components is put to sleep.

[Completed listing](#part0016_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_fb26e5e2e3e9fc2c_113c5)Run ItNow, if you click the start button, the window should show the changing times as the timer counts down to zero. The "Time's up!" message should appear when the timer reaches zero. You should also be able to close the window before the timer reaches 0, if you want to.Key Points and More

*   Runnable is a Java interface.
    *   An interface [declares](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_8f52562663593280_f878) the methods that must be defined by any class that will implement the interface.
    *   You will create your own new interface in later lessons.
*   One way to create a new thread is to implement the Runnable interface.
    *   The Runnable interface requires only one method, run().
    *   All threads require a method named run().
    *   Therefore, any class that is declared to implement the Runnable interface is guaranteed to have the run() method that is required for a thread.
*   How does one implement the Runnable interface?
    *   Include “implements Runnable” in the class declaration like this:

public class MyClass implements Runnable {

*   *   Add a run() method to the class. It should take no parameters and return nothing.
*   The constructor for a new Thread object has one parameter—a Runnable object. To create a thread in a class that implements the Runnable interface, use this as the parameter for the new thread's constructor, like this:

Thread thread = new Thread(this);

*   Start a thread by calling Thread's start() method. The start() method then calls the run() method of the class that implemented Runnable.
*   Does the pattern of code below look familiar?

EventQueue.invokeLater(new Runnable() {
  public void run() {
    new xxxx();
  }
});

*   You used that pattern in the main() method of this program and in all the programs you created in the More Do-It-Yourself Java Games book. That book described these lines of code as thread-related, with a promise to explain them in this book. Here are those explanations:
    *   The event dispatch thread (EDT) handles all window [events](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_3922a8ab0211a33d_fa62), such as mouse clicks and [keyboard input](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_ff1594eace1e8479_103b9). The EDT also handles a variety of system-wide window updates, such as when another program's window is moved across your program's window. Serious, unpredictable errors (such as thread interference or memory consistency errors) could occur if more than one thread tried to update a window component at the same time. Therefore, all updates to window components should be done in the EDT.
    *   Any program you write that works with a window component should use invokeLater() to run the program in the EDT.
    *   The book More Do-It-Yourself Java Games used EventQueue's invokeLater() method. This book uses SwingUtilities' invokeLater() method. You may use either one. SwingUtilities' invokeLater() calls EventQueue's invokeLater().
    *   invokeLater() requires a Runnable object as its parameter. It causes the Runnable object's run() method to be run in the EDT. The main() method in all the programs you created in this book and in the More Do-It-Yourself Java Games book called invokeLater(). invokeLater() created a new Runnable object with one method, run(), that called the rest of your code. Thus your code ran in the EDT.
*   The new Runnable object you created in TimerPanel runs its run() method code in a new thread and calls repaint(). So now both your new thread and the EDT update the timerPanel component. Might these updates from different threads cause one of the serious errors mentioned above? According to [www.oracle.com/technetwork/java/painting-140037.html](http://www.oracle.com/technetwork/java/painting-140037.html), Java uses one repaint manager to handle all repaint() and [revalidate](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_343d27f0427d700f_10b3a)() requests and places those requests on the queue for the EDT. So calling repaint() and revalidate() from multiple threads should not conflict, because they will all run in the EDT.

[Completed listing](#part0016_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_72707e3221164fa7_114ba)Run ItNow the window should show three rows of colors: the title and buttons should be on black bars and the timer on a dark pink bar.Key Points and More

*   Most threads should have a way to end naturally: either reach the end of code or end a loop.
*   You cannot actually stop a thread directly. All thread methods that previously stopped, suspended, resumed, and destroyed threads have been deprecated and should not be used. Instead, if you want to stop a thread before it reaches its natural end, you should interrupt the thread, then provide interrupt code to stop what the thread was doing.
*   To interrupt a thread that is sleeping, call Thread's interrupt() method. The call to sleep() should be wrapped in a try/catch block to catch an InterruptionException. Essentially, the code in that catch block will run when that Thread's interrupt() method is called.
*   Once a thread is stopped (it has returned from the run() method), it cannot be restarted. A new thread must be created and started in order to call the run() code again.
*   Each call to a Thread's constructor creates a new thread. Each thread runs independently, all running at the same time. To avoid multiple occurrences of a thread running simultaneously, stop the previous instance of the thread before starting a new one.
*   MyTimer is not a perfect timer. The length of time a thread sleeps may be affected by whatever else is running on the computer. The intervals between calls to sleep are also increased by how long the rest of the code on the thread runs before the thread sleeps again. Because computers are so fast, My Timer should work fine for most uses, but should not be relied upon if great precision is necessary.

Run ItWhen you double click the exported JAR file name, the program should run with the same results as before.Key Points and More

*   Audio files may be read through a URL. For example, to access an audio file named “Beep.wav” through a URL object named url, create a URL object set by getting the current class using the component's getClass() method and then getting the resource named “Beep.wav” using Class's getResource() method:

URL url = getClass().getResource("/Beep.wav");

*   *   This code will look for the file in the project's .bin directory when run in Eclipse.
    *   This code will look for the file in the program's .jar file when run outside of Eclipse.
    *   Provide a URL to Class's getResource() method, instead of providing an InputStream to Class's getResourceAsStream() method. Using an InputStream for audio files works in Eclipse, but not once the program is exported to the .jar file. Using a URL will work in both Eclipse and in the exported .jar file.
*   Next, access the URL object through an AudioInputStream. Get an AudioInputStream from the URL object using AudioSystem's getAudioInputStream() method. For example, to create an AudioInputStream object named audioInputStream, from a URL object named url:

AudioInputStream audioInputStream = AudioSystem.getAudioInputStream(url);

*   *   Trying to get the audio input stream will throw an UnsupportedAudioFileException if the file is not a supported audio file type, or an IOException if the file cannot be opened.
*   Manipulate the audio file through a Clip object. Create a Clip object, set by getting the clip from the audio system, using AudioSystem's getClip() method. For example, to create a Clip object named audioClip:

Clip audioClip = AudioSystem.getClip();

*   *   Trying to get the clip will throw a LineUnavailableException if resources are not currently available.
*   Before audio can be played, the clip must be opened to the AudioInputStream. To open a clip, use Clip's open() method. For example, to open a Clip object named audioClip to the AudioInputStream object named audioInputStream:

audioClip.open(audioInputStream);

*   *   Trying to open a clip will throw a LineUnavailableException if resources are not currently available or an IOException if the file cannot be opened.
*   Start or stop the audio using Clip's start() and stop() methods. For example, to start and stop the Clip object named audioClip:

audioClip.start();
audioClip.stop();

*   Audio files must be of type .wav or .au. 16-bit .wav files have worked best for me.
*   Audio files play on a separate thread. Therefore, the next line of code in your program may run while the audio file is being played.
*   Playing an audio file in a continuous loop will be covered in a later lesson.
*   Most of the audio files used in this book were downloaded from Pdsounds.org, a site of free public domain sound files, and then modified by me. All other audio files were created by Paul Godtland or me.
*   You can change the file format or volume of an audio file, or crop or edit audio files in other ways, with the free sound editor, Audacity. Download audacity from [http://sourceforge.net/projects/audacity/](http://sourceforge.net/projects/audacity/).

Project 2 - Speed WordsThis project will show you how to move objects with a mouse before later projects show you how to move objects with a thread.This project will also show you how to integrate the thread-controlled timer panel from My Timer into a game.The object of Speed Words is to rearrange letter tiles from a random seven-letter word, to form as many other valid words as you can in 60 seconds. Tiles may be dragged and dropped anywhere in the display. When a tile is dropped on another tile, the dropped tile will be connected to the tile onto which it was dropped. If the letters on the newly connected tiles form a new word, the tiles will be highlighted in yellow and the word will be added to the list of words you've formed. Points for each valid word are awarded by multiplying the length of the word by the sum of the point values of each letter in the word. Thus longer words result in a better score.Here is a screenshot of the Speed Words program:![](OEBPS/images/advanceddoityourselfjavagames_html_1f0653ef.jpg)  Lesson 2.1 - Drag Objects, Use a DictionaryTry It - Do Initial Setup for Speed Words

[Completed listing](#part0016_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_b477ba3d31fe7af8_1199b)Run ItAll newly formed words should be added to the list correctly now.Key Points and More

*   To allow the mouse to be used to drag an object on a panel, the object should have:
    *   Variables for keeping the object's x and y [coordinates](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_cbaf9bb1aae1460d_f803).
    *   A method to draw the object at its current x and y coordinates on a Graphics object.
    *   A method that checks whether x and y coordinates are inside the object at the object's current location.
    *   A method to set the object's x and y coordinates and then repaint the object.
    *   A method to change the object's x and y coordinates by the amount the object should move, and then repaint the object.
*   The panel object should use a mouse listener's mousePressed() method to check whether the mouse button is pressed down. mousePressed() should then:
    *   Get the position of the mouse event by calling MouseEvent's getX() and getY() methods.
    *   Check whether the mouse's x and y coordinates are inside the object at the object's current location. If the mouse position is inside the object, set a variable to indicate that the object has been designated as moving, and save the mouse's x and y coordinates.
        *   The Speed Words program uses the object itself to designate it as being moved, set to a value if the object is being moved, or set to null if the object is not being moved. You could instead use a boolean variable to keep track of whether or not the object is being moved.
*   The panel should use a mouse motion listener's mouseDragged() method to detect when the mouse is moved while the mouse's left button is down. mouseDragged() should then:
    *   Get the position of the mouse event by calling MouseEvent's getX() and getY() methods.
    *   If the moving object variable indicates that the object is moving, compare the mouse's new x and y coordinates with the saved x and y coordinates, then move the object that same amount by calling the object's method to change its coordinates.
    *   Repaint the panel.
*   The panel should use a mouse listener's mouseReleased() method to detect when the mouse button is released. mouseReleased() should then:
    *   If the moving object variable indicates that the object is being moved, set the moving object variable value to indicate the object is not being moved.
    *   Repaint the panel.
*   The panel's paintComponent() method should call the object's draw method with the panel's Graphics object.
*   The dictionary files used in this game are subsets of the file, enable1.txt, a free public domain file. The file enable1.txt may be downloaded from many different sites on the web, including [http://www.puzzlers.org/dokuwiki/doku.php?id=solving:wordlists:about:start&s=word%20list](http://www.puzzlers.org/dokuwiki/doku.php?id=solving:wordlists:about:start&s=word%20list).
*   The name of the file “enable” is an abbreviation for “Enhanced North American Benchmark LExicon”.
*   For more information, see the comments from the author of enable1.txt at [http://www.puzzlers.org/dokuwiki/doku.php?id=solving:wordlists:about:enable_readme](http://www.puzzlers.org/dokuwiki/doku.php?id=solving:wordlists:about:enable_readme).

Run ItWhen you double click the exported JAR file name, the program should run with the same results as before.Key Points and More

*   The TimerPanel from the My Timer Project may be used in any program that needs a countdown timer.
*   To customize the timer, extend the TimerPanel class, and call the constructor for TimerPanel (using [super()](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_2f458fc1a769be79_10d80)), passing it the required time and font values as arguments.
*   Override TimerPanel's timesUp() method to change what happens when the timer reaches 0\. Most often, timesUp() should call a method in the program.
    *   An overriding method cannot be less visible than the method it overrides. The timesUp() method must be set to protected or public to meet that requirement.

Project 3 - Match ThreeThe previous project showed how to use the mouse to move objects around in the window. This project will use a thread to automatically move objects.The object of Match Three is to swap balls to form chains of same-colored balls, in rows or columns. Chains of three or more balls will be removed and additional balls will drop down to take their places. Points are awarded based on the number of balls in a chain. A hint button is provided, but the program user loses points whenever he uses a hint.Here is a screenshot of the Match Three program:![](OEBPS/images/advanceddoityourselfjavagames_html_m17ad0f59.jpg)  Lesson 3.1 - Change the Mouse Icon DynamicallyChange the symbol used for the mouse so the user understands what action will be performed when the mouse is clicked.Try It - Do Initial Setup for Match Three

[Completed listing](#part0016_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_2ef14c0438b6c4ba_11cfa)Balls should be swapped when the user clicks the mouse in a location between two balls. Note, the clicked location is not between two balls if the location is nearest: the left edge of the first column, the right edge of the last column, the top edge of the first row, or the bottom edge of the last row. Otherwise, the ball in the clicked cell should be swapped with the ball in the adjacent cell along the clicked cell's edge closest to where the mouse was clicked.How can the program determine the closest edge of the selected cell?

*   Determine which cell was clicked.
*   Calculate how far the click was from each edge of the cell.
*   Check if the click was not in the first column and the left edge is closest.
*   Check if the click was not in the last column and the right edge is closest.
*   Check if the click was not in the first row and the the top edge is closest.
*   Check if the click was not in the last row and the bottom edge is closest.

[Completed listing](#part0016_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_652ce77a138204f2_11d2a)You now have the mouse click distances from the left, right, top, and bottom edges of the cell. To determine which edge the mouse click is closest to, calculate which distance is the smallest. For example, the mouse click is closest to the left edge, if the left distance is less than or equal to the right, top, and bottom distances. Ignore cases when the mouse is clicked near the left edge of the first column, near the right edge of the last column, near the top edge of the first row, or near the bottom edge of the last row.

[Completed listing](#part0016_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_935d9fe43a567699_11daa)Run ItNow as the mouse is moved across the window, the mouse cursor should display arrows indicating which balls will be swapped when clicked. If you click the mouse, the indicated balls should be swapped.Key Points and More

*   To set the mouse cursor, first create a cursor from one of the predefined cursors or create a custom cursor. The Java predefined cursors are:
    *   CROSSHAIR_CURSOR
    *   DEFAULT_CURSOR
    *   E_RESIZE CURSOR
    *   HAND_CURSOR
    *   MOVE_CURSOR
    *   N_RESIZE_CURSOR
    *   NE_RESIZE_CURSOR
    *   NW_RESIZE_CURSOR
    *   S_RESIZE_CURSOR
    *   SE_RESIZE_CURSOR
    *   SW_RESIZE_CURSOR
    *   TEXT_CURSOR
    *   W_RESIZE_CURSOR
    *   WAIT_CURSOR
*   For example, to create a cursor named busyCursor that displays as an hour glass:

Cursor busyCursor = new Cursor(Cursor.WAIT_CURSOR);

*   To set a cursor for a component, use the setCursor() method. For example, to switch to a cursor named busyCursor:

setCursor(busyCursor);

*   Any image may be used to create a custom cursor. The image will cover many pixels, but you may define any point within the image to represent the cursor location. For example, some cursors use the upper left corner of the image as the cursor location. Other cursors may use the center of the image as the cursor location.
*   To create a custom cursor, you'll need an image, the x, y coordinates in the image that represents the cursor's location, and a name for the cursor. For example, to create a new cursor from an [Image](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_8e0e9e83acafd60e_fe9a) object named myCursorImage, with the top left corner of the image being the x,y coordinates of the cursor location, and a name of “My cursor”:

Point hotSpot = new Point(0, 0);
Cursor customCursor = Toolkit.getDefaultToolkit().createCustomCursor(myCursorImage, hotSpot, "My cursor"));

*   Try to choose a cursor that most readily represents what you are trying to convey to the user.
*   If your code changes the cursor when the mouse is moved over a certain area of the window, or while something specific is happening, be sure to change the cursor back when the it leaves that area or after the activity is done. For example, continuing to use the busy cursor after the program is no longer busy could confuse the user into thinking your program just locked up his computer.

[Completed listing](#part0016_split_001.xhtml_anchor-0_1_c9dea525dfda5006_11eca)Run ItThe game should pause now, but it pauses before displaying marked chains and updating the score. These are the consequence of pausing the Event Dispatch Thread.Key Points and More

*   The code statements are in this order:

1.  1.  Mark all chains.
    2.  Repaint the panel.
    3.  Add to the score.
    4.  Pause.
    5.  Remove marked chains.
    6.  Repaint the panel again.

*   The pause code was placed in the step 4, before the marked chains are removed in step 5\. Why does the program seem to pause in step 2, before the first call to repaint?Remember the event dispatch thread (EDT) mentioned in the first project? All window component updates run on the EDT. The program's main code also runs on the EDT because the main() method creates the MatchThree object using SwingUtilities' invokeLater() method. The code sequence above actually runs as follows:

1.  1.  Mark all chains.
    2.  Send a request to paint the panel, but proceed immediately to the next line of code instead of waiting for the panel to repaint.
    3.  Send a request to update the score panel, but proceed immediately to the next line of code instead of waiting for the score panel to update.
    4.  Pause the thread (which in this case, happens to mean pause the EDT).
    5.  After the EDT is done pausing, the panel can finally be repainted and the score can be updated.
    6.  Remove marked chains.
    7.  Repaint the panel.

*   Pausing the EDT is a common error made by programmers the first time they try to use threads with Swing components. Pausing the EDT blocks requests to repaint and update components. To avoid such delays, run on a different thread any code that needs to pause activity.

Run ItWhen you double click the exported JAR file name, the program should run with the same results as before.Key Points and More

*   The first project [defined](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1222d6b11f73bdf2_f8f2) a thread by implementing the Runnable interface. This project defined an anonymous thread [inline](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_9cfe024df3ca3a62_ffea).
*   To define an anonymous thread inline:
    *   Create a new Thread object by calling its constructor. Do not assign the new thread to a variable.
    *   Define a new Runnable object as the argument to the new Thread's constructor. The Runnable object must include a public run() method that should take no parameters and return nothing.
    *   Place all the code for the new thread in run().
    *   Add .start() immediately after the ending curly bracket and parenthesis, }), that ended the creation of the new thread.
    *   For example: to place code in a new inline thread:

new Thread(new Runnable() {
  public void run() {
    (Place code here.)
  }
}).start();

*   Why did I implement the Runnable interface in the first lesson and use an inline thread in this lesson? In part to demonstrate two ways of creating Threads. In the first lesson I also wanted to call other thread methods, such as stop(). In this lesson, the only thread method needed is start(). If a thread need only be started, it is convenient to see the thread's run() method near the code that starts the thread.
*   The code could call other thread methods on a thread defined inline, if the thread is assigned to a variable. The thread would then not be anonymous. For example, to define inline a new Thread object named thread, then later start and stop thread:

Thread thread = new Thread(new Runnable() {
  public void run() {   
    (Place code here.)
  }
});
thread.start();
thread.stop();

*   If you used Java 7 instead of Java 8 in this lesson, you will receive a syntax error that you “Cannot refer to the non-final local variable xxx defined in an enclosing scope”. For example, to use a variable named count inside the thread, this won't work:

int count = 10;
new Thread(new Runnable() {
  public void run() {
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {

*   *   Instead, declare the variable count as final:

final int count = 10;
new Thread(new Runnable() {
  public void run() {
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {

*   *   Or, if you don't want to make count final (for example, if count is the number of times a target is hit, and that value changes as the user plays the game), you could make a copy of count and make the copy final:

final int c = count;
new Thread(new Runnable() {
  public void run() {
    for (int i = 0; i < c; i++) {

*   Parameters cannot be passed into a thread. However, information can be provided to a thread by declaring final variables outside of the thread, using one of the above techniques.

Project 4 - Baby BirdThe animation in this project is different from the animation in the previous projects in that the motion in this project will be continuous. Continuous motion is easily handled using a Java Swing [Timer](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_512f5e3af793b0a5_10f37). In this project, you'll also start using collision detection.The object of Baby Bird is to guide your bird through openings in walls, both large and small. The game will continuously move walls containing gaps across the window, moving from right to left. The bird will only move up or down. When you flap the bird's wings, the bird will move up. Otherwise, gravity will pull the bird down.Here is a screenshot of the Baby Bird program:![](OEBPS/images/advanceddoityourselfjavagames_html_20ef9f2f.jpg)  Lesson 4.1 - Animate with a Swing TimerTry It - Do Initial Setup for Baby Bird

But when gravity overtakes the rising action, the bird's wings should stop flapping and the bird should fall until you flap its wings again.Key Points and More

*   Java specifications recommend that you use Swing timers instead of separate threads to animate Swing objects.
*   Import Timer from javax.swing, not from java.util.
*   To create a Swing Timer, pass an integer interval and an action listener to its constructor.
    *   The interval is the number of milliseconds you want between each call to the intended action. 1000 milliseconds equals one second.
    *   What interval value should you use for object animation? The interval value used for the projects in this book were chosen by trial and error. Some use 40 milliseconds, some use 30, and some use 60\. With any new project, experiment with the interval values to see which gives more satisfactory results.
    *   You may define the action listener inline. The action listener must have a public actionPerformed() method that takes an ActionEvent parameter. The code within actionPerformed() will be repeated after each timer interval. For example, to create a timer named ticktock that will call move() every half second:

Timer ticktock = new Timer(500, new ActionListener() {
  public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) {
    move();
  }
});

*   To start a timer, call its start() method. To stop a timer, call its stop() method. For example, to start a timer named ticktock:

ticktock.start();

*   Swing timers work great with Swing objects. A Swing timer runs its code on a separate thread, places component updates on the EDT, and manages delays at set intervals without you needing to put a thread to sleep. These Swing timer behaviors prevent many of the errors warned about earlier that can otherwise occur when using Swing objects in threads.
*   Code using Swing timers is easier to write than code for threads.
*   Threads were introduced in this book before Swing timers to help you understand how threads work. All Java programs use separate threads to update Swing components, play sound, and run the main program logic. Having created your own threads, hopefully you now have a better understanding of why programs that update Swing components and play sound might cause code to run in a different order than you had expected.
*   The next few projects all use Swing timers. However, sometimes explicitly using a thread will work better than a Swing timer. An example of such a situation will be demonstrated in a later project.

[Completed listing](#part0016_split_001.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7b6076340694428b_124fd)Run ItA thud should play when a bird collides with a wall.Key Points and More

*   The easiest way to detect a collision between two objects is to check for an intersection between rectangles that represent the size and location of each object. For example, to create a new Rectangle object named boundingBox at 0, 10, having width 80 and height 40:

Rectangle boundingBox = new Rectangle(0, 10, 80, 40);

*   To test whether two rectangles intersect, use Rectangle's intersects() method. For example, to test whether a Rectangle object named obj1Rect intersects with a Rectangle object named obj2Rect:

if (obj1Rect.intersects(obj2Rect) {

*   A rectangle representation of an object may not be very precise, but using rectangles is a very fast means of testing for a collision. Collision detection with other shapes will be covered in a later lesson.

(Hint: use JOptionPane's showConfirmDialog() method, specifying this as its parent component, message as its message, “Play again?” as its title, and JOptionPane's YES_NO_OPTION variable as its option type.)
    3.  If option is a yes value: (Hint: use JOptionPane's YES_OPTION variable.)
        1.  Set the bird count for birdNestPanel to the difference LIVES minus 1\. (Hint: use BirdNestPanel's setBirdCount() method.)
        2.  Reset the score for scorePanel. (Hint: use ScorePanel's reset() method.)
        3.  Restart flightPanel. (Hint: use FlightPanel's restart() method.)
    4.  Otherwise:
        1.  Exit the program. (Hint: use System's exit() method, using 0 for the status value.)

Run ItWhen you double click the exported JAR file name, the program should run with the same results as before.Key Points and More

*   Animation flickers when the window isn't updated fast enough. The larger the area to update, the longer the program takes to paint and the more the animation will flicker.
    *   One way to reduce animation flicker is to repaint only the portions of the window that changed. Use repaint() with four parameters, x, y, width, and height, to repaint a rectangular portion of the window. For example to repaint a 100 x 50 area of a panel at 200, 220:

repaint(200, 220, 100, 50);

*   *   To repaint a moving object, repaint both the area to which the object moved as well the area from which the object left.
    *   Also, keep the methods that draw in the window as short and fast as you can. For example, calculate values outside of the paint routine and store them in instance variables, so the paint routine doesn't need to do the calculations.
    *   If your computer is fast enough, the running game's window may not have flickered much before you added the code intended to help reduce flickering. Flickering may be more pronounced on other computers, or you may need this knowledge if you later work on larger projects of your own.
*   You may find some websites that say you should add code to manually [double buffer](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_385a080466f2d085_f99d) the painting process in order to reduce animation flicker.
    *   Double buffering means all drawing is done on an off-screen image. Then the completed image is drawn in the window. This approach runs faster and more seamlessly than drawing directly to the window.
*   Swing components automatically do their own double buffering. Double buffering is turned on by default for JPanel.
*   To check whether double buffering is turned on for a Swing component, use:

isDoubleBuffered();

*   To turn on double buffering for a Swing component:

setDoubleBuffered(true);

*   A few other considerations for achieving smoother animation include:
    *   Keep the work that is done inside the animation loop as short and fast as you can.
    *   Move the object shorter distances and then update the object's position and repaint the object more frequently.
    *   Timing between updates controlled by the Swing Timer is not guaranteed. To achieve smoother animation, use a thread. Check the system time at the beginning of the thread, make the updates, check the time again, then calculate how much time to sleep to more accurately meet the desired interval between updates.

Project 5 - Falling BricksThis next project uses a timer that will be started and stopped multiple times. The project will also introduce abstract classes.The object of Falling Bricks is to maneuver falling bricks to complete rows of bricks that are then removed from the game. As the bricks fall, they may be moved left and right, rotated, or dropped. Points are earned for each completed row.Here is a screenshot of the Falling Bricks program:![](OEBPS/images/advanceddoityourselfjavagames_html_794b8c6b.jpg)  Lesson 5.1 - Use a Multi-Dimensional ArrayTry It - Do Initial Setup for Falling Bricks

The brick should look the same whether you rotate it left or right because the brick only has two states. Left or right rotation will become more apparent with other bricks.Key Points and More

*   Java arrays may be defined to use any number of dimensions. The number of dimensions equals the number of index values required to refer to a specific piece of information.
    *   For example, the contents of locations on a game board could be stored in a two-dimensional array, referred to by row and column indexes.
    *   For example, to-do list entries could be stored in a three-dimensional array, referred to by person, day, and location indexes.
    *   For example, the contents of locations in space and time could be stored in a four-dimensional array, referred to by x, y, z, and time indexes.
*   Java's multi-dimensional arrays are actually arrays of arrays. For example, the above two-dimensional array with rows and columns is maintained in Java as an array of rows, each containing an array of columns.
    *   Because each contained array is independent of any other contained array, each array of columns could hold a different number of elements. You saw this capability in the Falling Bricks program, where the three-dimensional TILES array had a different number of rows and columns for each state of the brick.
    *   An array whose contained arrays are all the same size could be defined by providing either the array sizes or initial values.
    *   An array whose contained arrays may have different sizes can only be defined by providing initial values.
*   To define an array by size, provide the size of each dimension in square brackets. For example, to define by size a 2x2 grid of booleans in an array named andResult:

boolean[][] andResult = new boolean[2][2];

*   To define an array by value, nest sets of values for each dimension within curly brackets, separating values and sets of values with commas. It is easier to visualize the data by grouping sets of values on different lines. For example, to define with initial values a 2 x 2 grid of booleans in an array named andResult:

boolean[][] andResult = {{true, false},
                         {false, false}};

*   Java stores data for arrays in “row-major” order. In other words, for a two-dimensional array defined with the first index as row and the second index as col, Java stores the elements for row 1, followed by the elements for row 2, etc.
*   If you use nested for loops to loop through all the elements in a multi-dimensional array, your code will run more efficiently if you loop through the first dimension (leftmost index) in the outermost loop, and the last dimension (rightmost index) in the innermost loop. For example, to loop through all the elements of a two-dimensional array named todo, whose indexes are person and day where person is the first index, loop through the person index in the outermost loop:

String todo[][] = new String[PEOPLE][DAYS];
for (int person = 0; person < PEOPLE; person++) {
  for (int day = 0; day < DAYS; day++) {
    todo[person][day] = "nothing yet";
  }
}Lesson 5.2 - Create an Abstract ClassAn abstract class is a class intended only for use as a superclass. Objects cannot be created from abstract classes.Try It - Create a TBrickAdd other methods needed in SBrick before you copy the SBrick code to create other bricks.Go back to SBrick.

Run ItWhen you double click the exported JAR file name, the program should run with the same results as before.Key Points and More

*   An abstract class is a class intended only for use as a superclass. Objects cannot be created from abstract classes.
*   You used abstract classes already. For example, Component is an abstract class. Because JButton and JPanel extend Component, Component's setFont() method can be used on either a JButton object or JLabel object. But because Component is abstract, a Component object cannot be created.
*   Use an abstract class for code that needs to individually refer to one of a group of classes by their superclass, but only if that code need never create an object of that superclass type. For example, even though an object of type Component cannot be created, JPanel's add() method requires a Component parameter, which can be any object that extends Component.
*   To define a class as abstract, include the abstract modifier in the class declaration. For example, to create an abstract class named Person:

public abstract class Person {
}

*   Use an abstract class that defines abstract methods when the classes that extend the class are required to have a particular method. For example, FileFilter is an abstract class. An object of type FileFilter cannot be created, but FileFilter could be extended, as you did when you created a class named ImageFileFilter in the More Do-It-Yourself Java Games book. However, in so doing, you were required to create two methods: accept() and getDescription(), in your new class. You were required to provide those methods because those methods are defined as abstract methods in the FileFilter class.
*   To define a method as abstract, include the abstract modifier in the method declaration, but do not provide code for the method. For example, to create an abstract method named getAge():

public abstract String getAge();

*   Abstract classes may or may not have abstract methods.
*   Abstract methods must be defined in an abstract class or in an interface. Interfaces will be discussed in a later lesson.
*   If a class extends a class that declares one or more abstract methods, the extending class must provide code for those abstract methods.

Project 6 - Gravity WellThis next project introduces state-driven programming. You will define a collection of possible states for the game, such as ready, flying, and crashed. You will write code to control the activity in each state and to determine when to change to a different state. This project also demonstrates how to detect collisions of non-rectangular shapes and how to control audio playback across several methods.The object of Gravity Well is to softly land a spaceship without crashing into rock walls. New landers will be provided after every crash or safe landing, as long as fuel remains. Fuel is replenished only after safe landings. The softer the landing and the more difficult the landing pad, the more points are awarded and the more fuel replenished.Here is a screenshot of the Gravity Well program:![](OEBPS/images/advanceddoityourselfjavagames_html_aa08940.jpg)  Lesson 6.1 - Use State-Driven Programming, Detect Collisions of Non-Rectangular ShapesTry It - Do Initial Setup for Gravity Well

[Completed listing](#part0016_split_002.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f6073047a3944fb_12ccf)Run ItThe multipliers for the landing pads should be much easier to read now.Try It - Add the Lander to the PanelThe lander is the little spaceship that needs to land on one of the landing pads. The lander has four images, one for drifting, and one each for moving right, left, and up.The lander must move whole pixels and its position will be updated every 30 milliseconds. In order to keep acceleration from changing the lander's movements too quickly, acceleration values will be much less than one. For this game, gravity will increase the lander's downward movement by .003 pixels every 30 milliseconds. Thruster acceleration will be five times the acceleration of gravity, or .015 pixels every 30 milliseconds. The maximum distance the lander can move in 30 milliseconds to land safely will be one quarter of a pixel, .25.Because gravity and acceleration will be calculated with decimal values, the x and y coordinates of the lander should be kept in double variables instead of integers.

1.  Copy the files, lander.gif, landerLeft.gif, landerRight.gif, and landerUp.gif, from where you downloaded them earlier as instructed near the start of this book, to the bin folder within the Gravity Well folder that is in your Java work folder.
2.  Create in the gravitywell package a new class named Lander, which uses no superclass and has no stub code.
3.  Add a private static final string variable named IMAGE_DRIFT, set to “/lander.gif”.
4.  Add a private static final string variable named IMAGE_LEFT, set to “/landerLeft.gif”.
5.  Add a private static final string variable named IMAGE_RIGHT, set to “/landerRight.gif”.
6.  Add a private static final string variable named IMAGE_UP, set to “/landerUp.gif”.
7.  Add a private static final integer variable named MOVE_DRIFT, set to 0.

15.  Add a private static final double variable named GRAVITY, set to .003d.
16.  Add a private static final double variable named ACCELERATION, set to .015d.

To ease programming such code, define different game states, then write code to handle each state. The timer loop may then simply check the game state and call appropriate code.Code to manage game states could be written using a couple different approaches. This project will demonstrate the easiest way, using a switch block. The more difficult but more efficient coding technique uses an interface and will be demonstrated in the next project.Go back to GamePanel.Define each of the possible state values and a variable to hold the current state.

Run ItWhen you double click the exported JAR file name, the program should run with the same results as before.Key Points and More

*   Video games, in which many different actions or reactions may be needed in any order, are often written using state-driven programming.
*   State-driven programming controls activity based on the state of the game.
*   Code written using state-driven design often results in cleaner, more organized, and easier to read and write code.
*   Sate-driven code could be written a couple different ways. The easiest way to write state-driven code is to use a switch block:
    *   Define static final integer variables for each state, each with a unique integer value.
    *   Define an integer instance variable set to the current state of the program, using one of the static instance variables.
    *   Use a switch block to check the value of the current state variable, usually within a timer loop, and call the correct method to handle the current state.
    *   Within the method that handles the state, update the state if conditions changed.
*   Another technique, using an interface, will be demonstrated in the next project. State-driven programming with an interface is more efficient, allows for more features, and runs faster, but is also more complicated to write.
*   Collisions are often detected by getting the rectangular bounds of two objects and then checking whether they intersect. But that doesn't work well for irregularly shaped objects. Here are other techniques used to detect collisions between irregularly shaped objects. The first two techniques were demonstrated in this project:
    *   If one object is a Polygon and the other is a Rectangle. Use Polygon's intersects() method.
    *   If one object is a rectangle and the other is a vertical or horizontal line, simply compare where each side of the rectangle resides in relation to the line.
    *   If one object is a rectangle and the other is a line at any angle, as long as you know the endpoints of the line, use Rectangle's intersectsLine() method.
    *   If both objects are Polygons, convert them to Areas. Use Area's intersect() method to get a new Area object made up of where the two Polygons intersected. (Hint: the method is named intersect(), not intersects().) If the new Area object is empty, the two Polygons did not intersect. (Hint: use Area's isEmpty() method.)

Project 7 - Cat and MouseThis next project teaches you how to create an interface to produce more efficient state-driven code. This project also demonstrates how to create and use custom exceptions.The object of Cat and Mouse is for you, as the mouse, to eat all the cheese in the maze without the cat catching you. But be careful - the cat can hear you when you move and will try to hunt you down.Here is a screenshot of the Cat and Mouse program:![](OEBPS/images/advanceddoityourselfjavagames_html_110422bc.jpg)  Lesson 7.1 - Use System Exit CodesSystem [exit codes](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f4f74038439e07f9_fb48) are used to indicate whether the program exited as expected.Try It - Do Initial Setup for Cat and Mouse

Be sure to put the file name back to “/maze.txt” before going on to the next step.Key Points and More

*   System's exit() method closes all open windows and ends the program. Any integer value may be used for the method's exit code parameter. Specifying different exit codes for different errors may be helpful for more quickly determining what went wrong when an error occurs.
*   Exit codes do not affect how the program code runs. However, the exit code could possibly be used by some other program that runs the program. Such a program may check the exit code from the program to see whether the program ended normally.
*   If you expect your program to some day be run by another program, you should document what you chose for your program's exit codes and what each exit code means.
*   If you don't expect your program to some day be run by another program, follow these recommended guidelines for exit codes:
    *   Use 0 for a normal end of the program. For example, use 0 if the window is being closed because the program asked the user whether he wanted to play again and he chose to not play again.
    *   Use a positive integer if the program ended due to an error the code was written to catch, such as a required file can't be found.
    *   Use a negative integer if the program ended due to an unexpected error.

[Completed listing](#part0016_split_002.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e619ba9a8d930181_131c0)Run ItThe maze should now appear in the window with cheese in all but the first cell. If you want, you may edit the maze.txt file to use a different maze. Use a capital X for walls, a blank for an empty path, a period for a path with a piece of cheese in it, a capital M for where you want the mouse to start, a capital C for where you want the cat to start, and lowercase m's where you want the extra mice to wait for their turn. You can also make the maze any size you want by changing the number of rows or columns in the maze.txt file. But all rows must have the same number of characters.Try It - Handle Invalid Maze CharactersWhat happens if the maze.txt file contains characters other than capital X, M, C, lowercase m, blank, or period? The program happens to draw any such cell as an empty path. However, since the cell is not assigned a proper integer value, the cell without a value may cause other problems later. A better solution would be to require that all maze files use only the allowed characters.One way to handle invalid input data would be for the code that reads the data to throw an exception, much like other file input methods throw exceptions.First, create a class that extends Exception, naming the class for the error the class represents.

1.  Create in the catandmouse package a new class named InvalidMazeCharacterException, which uses Exception as its superclass and has no stub code.
2.  Use Quick Fix to add a private static final long integer variable named serialVersionUID, set to 1L.
3.  Add a private static final string variable named MESSAGE1, set to “Invalid maze character ”.
4.  Add a private static final string variable named MESSAGE2, set to “ in file ”.
5.  Add a private character variable named invalidCharacter, not initialized.
6.  Add a private string variable named fileName, not initialized.

Listing 7-25, from InvalidMazeCharacterException.java

* * *

package annette.godtland.catandmouse;

If a row is too short, an ArrayIndexOutOfBounds run time error will occur. If a row is too long, the last characters will be ignored. Either way, the maze wouldn't appear as was likely intended.A better solution would be to require that all maze files have all records the same length. [Completed listing](#part0016_split_002.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d47f81ab2742455c_13300)Run ItA small black mouse, facing down, should appear in the top left corner of the path in the maze.Key Points and More

*   Create your own custom exceptions by using Exception as the superclass. For example, to create an exception named InvalidDataException:

public Class InvalidDataException extends Exception {

*   The constructor for the custom exception should call Exception's constructor, passing a string, the message to display for the exception, as an argument. For example, the first line of the constructor for a custom invalid data exception should be:

super("Invalid Data");

*   If additional details about the error can be provided for a custom exception, define instance variables to hold those details and a constructor that expects values for those variables. For example, for InvalidDataException to explain what invalid data was used, the InvalidDataException class constructor might take a string parameter that contains the invalid data, to display that string in a message:

private String invalidData;
public InvalidDataException(String invalidData) {
  super(invalidData + " is not allowed.");
  this.invalidData = invalidData;
}

*   To use a custom exception in your program, create the exception by calling its constructor, then throw the exception. For example, to throw a new InvalidDataException if a string named name contains more than 10 characters:

if (name.length() > 10) {
  throw new InvalidDataException(name);
}

*   If code throws an InvalidDataException, code elsewhere must catch the InvalidDataException.
    *   The code that throws the exception is often within a try/catch block. For example, to display a message if an InvalidDataException is thrown:

try {
  if (name.length() > 10) {
    throw new InvalidDataException(name);
  }
}
catch (InvalidDataException e) {
  String message = e.getMessage();
  JOptionPane.showMessageDialog(null, message);
}

*   *   Alternatively, a method could be declared to throw the exception. But then any code that calls the method must handle the exception. For example, if a method named getName() retrieves text from a text input field named nameField and should throw an InvalidDataException to its calling method if the user entered more than 10 characters:

public string getName() throws InvalidDataException {
  String name = nameField.getText();
  if (name.length() > 10) {
    throw new InvalidDataException(name);
  }
  return name;
}

*   *   *   Note, this method has no try/catch block because the method itself throws the exception to the code that calls getName().
        *   Any code that calls getName() must handle the exception, either by wrapping the call to getName() in a try/catch block then catching an InvalidDataException, or by throwing the InvalidDataException to be caught by the previous level of code. Eventually, some block of code must catch the exception.
*   Another often-used technique not demonstrated in this lesson is to call Exception's printStackTrace() method. That method will print a stack trace to the console. A stack trace is the exception's message followed by a list of each class and method call that preceded the exception, much like the stack traces you've seen in Eclipse's console when your code hit a run time error, such as a null pointer exception or an index out of bounds exception.
    *   The programs in these books have all used a graphical user interface. Stack traces printed to the console would not normally be seen by anyone running these games. That is why I usually use JOptionPane to show a message dialog instead of calling Exceptions printStackTrace() method for programs like these.
    *   Printing the stack trace for your own use is sometimes helpful as you write the program. A stack trace may help you determine why an exception was thrown when you weren't expecting the exception.
*   You may notice that methods were defined to get the values of the custom exceptions' instance variables, but the methods were never called. Providing such methods allows code that catches the exception to construct its own message or to check those values to determine what the program should do next. Those methods may be useful in other programs.

The mouse will repeatedly perform an action while in each state. But some code should be run only once: every time the mouse enters or exits each state. Therefore three methods should be defined for each state: enter(), performAction(), and exit(). How do you ensure that those methods are defined for all states? Use an Interface.

So far, the code defined a MouseRunState class, but the program hasn't created a MouseRunState object. Running the program at this point is just to verify that the code changes you made didn't cause any problems.Key Points and More

*   You've been using interfaces in many of the other programs. For threads, you've used the Runnable interface, with its required run() method. For buttons, you've used the ActionListener interface, with its required actionPerformed() method. In all cases the interfaces required that you provide code for certain methods.
*   In this program, you created a new interface named State to ensure that classes implementing State provide code for enter(), performAction(), and exit() methods.
*   To create a new interface, declare an interface instead of a class. For example, to create an interface named Movable:

public interface Movable {
}

*   Declare each method required for an interface, followed by a semi-colon. No curly brackets should appear after the declaration, and no code should be provided to implement the method. For example, to declare a public method named mouseClicked() that takes two parameters—an integer named x, an integer named y—and returns nothing:

public void mouseClicked(int x, int y);

*   To use an interface, a class declaration must state that it implements the interface and it must define all the methods declared by the interface. For example, for a class named GamePiece to implement Movable, which declares the method above named mouseClicked():

public class GamePiece implements Movable {
  private int x;
  private int y;
  public void MouseClicked(int x, int y) {
    this.x = x;
    this.y = y;
  }
}

*   Did the explanation of how to define the methods for an interface sound familiar? Methods are defined in the same way for an abstract class, except method declarations for an abstract class include the “abstract” modifier. For both abstract classes and interfaces, Java ensures that the extended or implementing class provides code for those declared methods.
    *   Could State have been defined as an abstract class with abstract methods instead of being defined as an interface? Yes.
    *   Why did I make State an interface instead of an abstract class in the Cat and Mouse program? When a code construct could be defined as either an abstract class or an interface, it is more appropriate to define it as an interface if its functionality is something that might be added to any kind of object. For example, a run() method could be required by a CatAndMouse object and by a MyTimer object, even though those two objects don't have much else in common. A State is something that could be added to any kind of object for which a programmer wants to track its state.
    *   What issues might arise if you define a code construct as an abstract class instead of as an interface? By making a class abstract, you take away its subclasses's ability to inherit behavior from any other classes. A Java class can have only one superclass but may implement multiple interfaces. For example, if classes named Animal, Runnable, and Movable were all defined as abstract classes, a Dog class could extend only one of those classes. However, if instead Runnable and Movable were defined as interfaces, you could declare a Dog class that extends Animal and implements both Runnable and Movable:

public class Dog extends Animal implements Runnable, Movable {
}

*   *   When deciding between defining a construct as an abstract class or as an interface, choose an abstract class if any class that will use it actually should be that type of object. For example, a Vehicle should probably be an abstract class if it will be used by a Car, which actually is a type of Vehicle. Make the class an interface if the class simply describes behavior that might be used by a variety of object types. For example, Transporter could be an interface used by cars or elevators.
    *   When must a code construct be defined as an abstract class instead of an interface? When the code construct should provide a default implementation for at least one of its methods.
