            1.  If intoY is greater than the offsetY element at index direction:
                1.  Add a comment about centering in the next cell.
                2.  Set y to the result of y minus intoY, plus the size of the cell. (Hint: use Maze's CELL_SIZE variable.)
        3.  If the value is DIRECTION_LEFT:
            1.  If intoX is greater than the offsetX element at index direction:
                1.  Add a comment about centering in this cell.
                2.  Set x to the difference x minus intoX.
    4.  If the value is DIRECTION_RIGHT:
        1.  1.  If intoX is greater than the offsetX element at index direction:
                1.  Add a comment about centering in the next cell.
                2.  Set x to the result of x minus intoX, plus the size of the cell. (Hint: use Maze's CELL_SIZE variable.)

[Completed listing](#part0016_split_003.xhtml_anchor-0_1_584ce11f19aba467_13770)Run ItThe cat should wander as before, but now when you press a cursor movement key, the cat should hunt at the same speed as the mouse. However, if you hold the cursor movement key down, the cat moves faster than the mouse.Try It - Do Not Set to the Same State Twice.If you examine your code, you should see that the code never increases the speed beyond SPEED_HUNT. So how can the cat move faster? Holding a keyboard key down generates multiple key pressed events before the key is released. The code sets the state of cat to STATE_HUNT every time a key pressed event occurs. The setState() method first calls the state's exit() method before setting the new state. The exit() method centers the cat in the cell, moving the cat forward a little more than its speed would normally take it. Thus, repeatedly centering the cat in the cell results in the cat moving faster. To fix this problem, make sure you never set any maze runner to the same state twice.Go back to MazeRunner.In setState():

1.  Wrap all the code in the method into an if block that is only run if newState is not equal to state().

      state = newState;
      state.enter();
    }
  }
    ...

Run ItWhen you double click the exported JAR file name, the program should run with the same results as before.Key Points and More

*   State-driven programs could be controlled by if/else blocks, switches, or by state objects that implement a common interface.
*   If/else blocks and switch blocks are easier to write for small programs with fewer states. But in a program with a large number of states, controlling how and when to switch between states is harder using if/else blocks or switch blocks. Also, because the state must be checked every time through the game loop, a large number of states may slow down the game.
*   State objects that implement a common State interface might be more efficient because the game loop never has to test the game's state. The game automatically calls the correct code for the state, by calling one of the required methods in the State interface.
*   It is also easy to add additional states to a program that uses state objects, without affecting code already written for the other states. Often if you need to add states to a program controlled by a switch block, corresponding changes must also be made to the code that handles other states.
*   State objects allow more features than a switch block because each state can implement several possible actions. This project had methods for entering the state, performing a repeatable action in the state, and exiting the state. Depending on the kind of object for which you are providing the states, you might require different methods or different numbers of methods than the states used to implement this game. For example, the game itself might have game states that implement methods named run(), and updateData().
*   To use state objects for state-driven programming, first create an interface to define the state, naming all of its required methods. For example, to create an interface named GameState with methods named run() and updateData():

public interface GameState {
  public void run();
  public void updateData();
}

*   Next, implement that interface in classes, one for each possible state. Each state must then provide code for all the methods in the interface. For example, a game may have a load state, a play game state, and an end game state. To create a state named LoadState:

public class LoadState implements GameState {
  public void run () {
    ...
  }
  public void updateData () {
    ...
  }
}

*   Next, your program should create instance variables for each state and an instance variable to hold the current state. For example, if possible state classes are named LoadState, PlayGameState, and EndGameState, and they all implement the interface named GameState, and you want to store the current state, loadState, in an instance variable named currentState:

public LoadState loadState = new LoadState();
public PlayGameState playGameState = new PlayGameState();
public EndGameState endGameState = new EndGameState();
public GameState currentState = loadState

*   Next, your game loop should call one or more of the methods on the variable that holds the current state. For example, calling the run() method on the above defined currentState will result in calling the run() method of loadState(), playGameState(), or endGameState(), depending on which object was most recently assigned to currentState:

currentState.run();

*   Finally, the code that runs for each state should change the state when necessary. For example, if the game should end when pieces is 0:

if (pieces == 0) {
  currentState = endGameState;
}

*   The Cat and Mouse program added a step to the above process. Changing state needed to always first run the code to exit the previous state, then set the state to the new state, then run the code to enter the new state. If setting the state should perform a sequence of steps, provide a method to set the state. For example, if changing the GameState should always call updateData() from the old state before switching to a new state, use

private void setState(GameState newGameState) {
  currentState.updateData();
  currentState = newGameState();
}Project 8 - BlitzIn this project, you'll learn to separate program logic from user interface implementation, using a model/view/controller design.The [model](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_bca0387e5a348c25_106a4) contains the logic of the game, but no user interface. The model defines objects, including a deck of cards and multiple players, but cannot draw those objects. The model also controls the flow of the game using state-driven design, based on the rules for playing Blitz.The [view](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_9625e49bae9e0ad0_11070) is a JFrame with panels and buttons. Without game logic, the view displays just text, images, and shapes, and can move them around on the screen. The view also recognizes mouse clicks, which is how the user enters his choices.The model and view communicate with each other through the [controller](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c3c33d34cfa62c1_f7cd). The controller must convert the card objects into images, tell the view what must be moved on the screen based on instructions from the model, and tell the model what action to take based on choices made by the user in the view.Blitz, also known as Scat or 31, is a card game with a goal to get 31 points in one suit, or rap, a signal that you think someone else has a worse hand than you. Players lose one of their three tokens every time they lose to a blitz or rap. But beware, if the player who raps also has the worst hand, he must pay double.Here is a screenshot of the Blitz program:![](OEBPS/images/advanceddoityourselfjavagames_html_m442416f5.jpg)  Lesson 8.1 - Lay out the Display in the “View”Try It - Do Initial Setup for BlitzCreate separate packages for the model, view, and controller to make it easier to use the model with different views and controllers later.

Each player's area should show the player's name, up to 4 cards below his name, up to 3 tokens below the cards, and additional text information below the tokens. A 4-pixel space should be displayed between cards, a gap of 20 pixels should be displayed between players, and a margin of 10 pixels should be shown around the edges of the window. The text will have a font size of 20, and cards will be the height of the images in the BlitzController class. The spacing and font size will be used by another class, so should be public.

1.  Create in the blitz.view package a new class named GamePanel, which uses JPanel as its superclass and has no stub code.
    1.  Use Quick Fix to add a private static final long integer variable named serialVersionUID, set to 1L.
    2.  Add a public static final integer variable named SPACING, set to 4.
    3.  Add a private static final integer variable named GAP, set to 20.
    4.  Add a private static final integer variable named MARGIN, set to 10.
    5.  Add a public static final integer variable named FONT_SIZE, set to 20.
    6.  Add a private static final integer variable named CARD_WIDTH, set to the width of a card in BlitzController. (Hint: use BlitzController's CARD_WIDTH variable.)
    7.  Add a private static final integer variable named CARD_HEIGHT, set to the height of a card in BlitzController. (Hint: use BlitzController's CARD_HEIGHT variable.)
    8.  Add a private static final integer variable named PLAYER_WIDTH, set to the width of 4 cards plus the spacings between them. (Hint: use CARD_WIDTH and SPACING.)
    9.  Add a private static final integer variable named PLAYER_HEIGHT, set to a card height, 3 rows of text, plus the spacings between them. (Hint: use CARD_HEIGHT, FONT_SIZE, and SPACING.)
    10.  Add a private static final integer variable named WIDTH, set to 2 player widths, a gap between them, plus a margin on each side of the window. (Hint: use PLAYER_WIDTH, GAP, and MARGIN.)
    11.  Add a private static final integer variable named HEIGHT, set to the total of: 2 player heights, a card height, gaps above and below the middle card, and margins at the top and bottom of the window. (Hint: use PLAYER_HEIGHT, CARD_HEIGHT, GAP, and MARGIN.)

[Completed listing](#part0016_split_003.xhtml_anchor-0_1_68bf8f222cf8a9f1_13ad2)In the game of Blitz, a player may continue playing even when he has no tokens. However, if such a player is supposed to lose one or more tokens, theoretically resulting in a number of tokens less than zero, he would be out of the game. A player having no tokens is considered to be “Riding” and a player who would have a negative value for tokens is considered to be “Out”. Create three players named “Tom”, “Dick”, and “Harry”, with 3, 0, and -1 tokens, respectively.Go back to BlitzController.In the BlitzController constructor:

3.  Set the player for gamePanel at index 2 to be named “Harry” and have a value of -1 as the number of tokens. (Hint: use GamePanel's setPlayer() method.)

[Completed listing](#part0016_split_003.xhtml_anchor-0_1_364738e3b932bc1e_13b62)Run It“Rapped” should now appear below Tom's tokens.Key Points and More

*   The view presents the game information to the user and is how the user provides input into the game.
*   The controller contains the main() method, tells the view what to add or update in the display, requests user input from the view, and responds to user input from the view.
*   The view for the Blitz game is a Java Swing view, using a JFrame and other components. The Swing components can display only text, images, and shapes, but can move them around on the screen as directed by the controller. The Swing components can also monitor for mouse clicks and other events.
*   The view should include no game logic, only details of how the window is laid out for the user to interact with the game.

[Completed listing](#part0016_split_003.xhtml_anchor-0_1_509de0638b749670_13bd2)The loop you just created runs only once because the loop is defined to stop when the card is moving, and the code in the loop sets the card to not moving.Next, check if the card has reached its x destination or y destination. If it has not yet reached either destination, the card should continue moving.The card will have reached its x destination if the card is moving to the right and its current location is greater than the final x destination, or if it is moving to the left and its current location is less than the final x destination. In either case, set the card's current x location to the desired final x location. If the card has not yet reached its x destination, it should continue moving.The card will have reached its y destination if the card is moving down and its current location is greater than the final y destination, or if it is moving up and its current location is less than the final y destination. In either case, set the card's current y location to the desired final y location. If the card has not yet reached its y destination, it should continue moving.In moveCard(),

1.  Move the remaining two comments, about stopping movement, to the end of the while loop.
2.  After the comment to stop X movement if the X movement went too far:
    1.  If incrementX is greater than 0 and cardX is greater than endX, or if incrementX is less than 0 and cardX is less than endX:
        1.  Set cardX to endX.
    2.  Otherwise:
        1.  Set cardIsMoving to true.
3.  After the comment to stopY movement if the Y movement went too far:
    1.  If incrementY is greater than 0 and cardY is greater than endY, or if incrementY is less than 0 and cardY is less than endY:
        1.  Set cardY to endY.
    2.  Otherwise:
        1.  Set cardIsMoving to true.

[Completed listing](#part0016_split_003.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d634eee1799a49b0_13ca2)Run ItThe game should run the same as before, except after the ace of hearts disappears, Tom should show only 1 token remaining and “Rapped Lost 2” should be displayed below his token.Key Points and More

*   One way to slow down animation is by putting the thread to sleep between each iteration of the animation loop. Another way is to use a Timer. Both were demonstrated in earlier lessons in this book.
*   Why did I put the thread to sleep instead of use a Timer in this game? A timer uses a background thread, which allows the main thread to continue running while the timer thread runs. In contrast, this game must pause while a card is moved. Otherwise, the next card movement would start before the first card movement was completed.
*   Calling SwingUtilities' invokeLater() method from main() placed the main thread of this program on the EDT. As you learned earlier, doing so is advised for any program that uses Java Swing.
*   Calling Thread's sleep() method on the main thread puts the EDT to sleep, which is not advised for any program that uses Java Swing because doing so blocks the EDT. No other window updates can be made nor can any other events be responded to while the the EDT is sleeping. You may have noticed that if you try to close the window for Blitz, the window won't close until the program has finished dealing the cards.
    *   As you saw in this lesson, putting the thread to sleep from the constructor interrupted painting the initial window.
        *   One way to solve this is to wait until after the window is constructed and visible before the thread is put to sleep. This could be accomplished by starting the game from a button on the window, or in response to a message displayed from a JOptionPane.
        *   Another way would be to start a new thread to call the method that puts the thread to sleep. Then the new thread instead of the EDT would be put to sleep.
*   Swing combines multiple repaint requests into one if they are submitted closely together. To ensure that one repaint is processed completely before a following repaint is processed, use paintImmediately() instead of repaint().
*   Animation may be slowed down by using one of several techniques:
    *   Use a Timer. This prevents conflicts with the EDT. However, be aware that the timer runs on a different thread. The current thread will continue running while the code in the run() method of the timer is running.
    *   Use Thread.sleep(). However, be aware that if code does this from the EDT, other repaint and event requests will be blocked until until the thread is done sleeping.
    *   Use paintImmediately() instead of repaint(). This will force the paint request, but will still block the EDT from processing any previously submitted repaint and event requests.
    *   Run in a different thread the code that calls the animation loop. However, be aware that the new thread will run concurrently with other threads. Be sure to put all the code that you want to run in sequence in a single thread. For example, to move a card from the deck to a player and then move another card from that same player to the discard, both steps could run in one thread, both calling the same move() method. However, if processing the next player is not on the same thread, the next player might take his turn before the first player's turn is done. Both players might then move a card at the same time.
    *   Run in a different thread the code that calls the animation loop, and synchronize the method that has the animation loop. To synchronize a method, use the synchronized modifier in the method declaration. For example, to synchronize the move() method:

private synchronized void move(int beginX, int beginY, int endX, int endY) {

*   *   A synchronized method is locked when accessed so only one thread can access it at a time. However, if a method is called by more than two threads, the order the threads happen to access the method is not guaranteed.Synchronizing the loop to move the card could not be used for the Blitz project because players must not be allowed to play out of turn. The Blitz project uses one thread for players and one thread for the animation loop. If players 1, 2, and 3 sequentially try to move a card, player 1 will move a card. Because the animation loop is on a separate thread, player 2 will try to move next but can't because player 1 has a lock on moving the card. And now player 3 takes his turn. But if player 1 isn't done moving yet, and both player 2 and player 3 are waiting to move the card, there is no guarantee who gets to move the card first.
    *   Place the entire process in a separate thread. For example, I could have placed all the code that runs in the BlitzModel on a separate thread, thus ensuring that everything ran in sequence and in the correct order. But then much more code would have been required to make sure all Swing components were created and handled on the EDT.
    *   Threads can be managed with other techniques, but those techniques are beyond the scope of this book.

[Completed listing](#part0016_split_003.xhtml_anchor-0_1_ad2bdd08aadc634d_13ed2)Because this project uses a large number of states, an interface would be better than a switch block for managing the state. However, the intent of this project is to demonstrate how to separate the user interface from the game logic. Managing the state with an interface would involve creating many more classes and make this program much larger than what is needed to teach the intended lesson. Therefore, use the easier-to-write switch block to manage the game state.Add a method that calls the appropriate method based on the state of the game.

Play should then continue on to the next player. Play should continue clockwise one full round after someone raps, or end immediately if someone gets a blitz, 31 points in his hand.Try It - Settle a RapA player must rap before drawing a card. If a player raps, he does not get to draw a card, and play should move to the next player, continuing in clockwise order. After someone raps, each other player should get one more turn. When play gets back to the person who rapped, points are calculated for everyone's hand. The player with the fewest points loses 1 token. If no one has fewer points than the player who rapped, the player who rapped should lose 2 tokens and no one else lose any tokens, even if they have the same number of points as the player who rapped.After the rap is settled, the next player to the left of the current dealer and still in the game should be the next dealer.Go back to BlitzModel.

1.  Add a public method named getNextDealerId(). It should take no parameters and return an integer.
    1.  Create a boolean named done, set to false.
    2.  Create an integer named nextDealerId, set to the result of the sum dealerId plus 1, modulo numberOfPlayers.
    3.  While done is false:
        1.  If the players element at index nextDealerId is not out: (Hint: use Player's isOut() method.)
            1.  Set done to true.
        2.  Otherwise:
            1.  Set nextDealerId to the result of the sum nextDealerId plus 1, modulo numberOfPlayers.
    4.  Return nextDealerId.

            3.  Make controller show the blitz for the players element at index dealTo. (Hint: use BlitzController's showBlitz() method.)
            4.  Set state to STATE_SETTLE_BLITZ.
4.  After the loop that deals the cards, wrap the five lines of code, which deal the discard and set the state, into an if block that only runs if blitz is false. (Hint: include the comment but do not include the call to play().)

When the next hand is dealt, the cards should be dealt face down once again.Key Points and More

*   Model/view/controller design organizes code into 3 separate categories:
    *   The model holds the game objects and controls the flow of action based on the rules of the game.
    *   The view presents the game information to the user and allows user input into the game.
    *   The controller provides interpretation of the data and the flow of information between the model and the view.
*   For every action the model takes that the program user should be aware of, the model must notify the controller. The controller must then notify the view of the action, after converting the data provided by the model into a form the view can use.
*   For every action the user takes with the view, the view must notify the controller. The controller must then notify the model, after converting the data provided by the view into a form the model can use.
*   In the Blitz game:
    *   The model has a deck of cards and multiple players. The model also controls the flow of the game using state-driven design, based on the rules for playing Blitz.
    *   The view is a Java JFrame that can display text, images, and shapes, and can move them around in the window. The view also recognize mouse clicks, which is how the user enters his choices.
    *   The controller must convert the card objects into images, tell the view what must be presented and moved in the window based on instructions from the model, and tell the model what action to take based on choices made by the user.
*   Some programmers disagree whether the controller or the model should contain the game loop that controls the flow of the game. I chose to put the game loop in the model because I see the flow of the program as very much part of the logic and rules of the game. I wanted to contain all the logic of the game in the model, leaving the controller to only interpret and send information back and forth between the view and the model. This game might have been easier to write had I put game flow into the controller rather than in the model. But I think the model is easier to reuse if the game flow is in the model.
*   Some programmers disagree whether or not the objects should be used to pass data into the view. For example, this game would have been a lot easier to write if the controller had passed the Card and Player objects to the View instead of converting them to BufferedImages and integer IDs. But again, I think the controller and view might be easier to reuse for other games if the controller and view are not so specifically tied to the Blitz Card and Blitz Player.
*   You may choose to separate the model, view, and controller code differently for other programs.
*   Using a model/view/controller design makes it much easier to create additional versions of the game to run with different user interfaces.
    *   This Blitz game runs using a Java Swing user interface so the game could be run on a computer that uses a Windows, MAC OSX, or Linux operating system.
    *   You could use the same model with a different view and controller to create a text version or 3-D version of the game.
    *   Or you could use the same model with a different view and controller to create the game as an app for an Android device.
    *   Or maybe some day you could use the same model with a different view and controller to play the game against a robot.
    *   In all cases, the logic of the game would remain the same and is already neatly bundled in the model.
*   Using the model/view/controller design makes it easier to divide a larger project across a team. The user interface and game logic could easily be written by different people.
*   Using the model/view/controller design makes it easier to adapt the view for other projects. The BlitzView could easily be adapted for more players, for games that need areas to lay down cards, use decks of cards with different point values, and more.
*   Using the model/view/controller design results in a much larger program. The Blitz game could have been much easier to write, using a lot less code, if each object combined its own logic and view, much like the previous programs in this book. But then the program wouldn't have had any of the advantages listed above.

Lesson 8.5 - Reuse Game LogicSince you've completely separated the Blitz game logic from the user interface, the logic could be used with any other user interface. Each new user interface (view) would require a new controller to handle communications between the model and the view. In this lesson you'll prepare the Blitz model to be used with a different controller.Try It - Provide an Interface for the Blitz ControllerCreate an Interface for all the controller methods required by the Blitz model.

1.  Rename the BlitzController class to BlitzControllerSwing. (Hint: to easily rename within Eclipse a class and all references to the class, right click the class name in the Package Explorer, choose Refactor / Rename..., and enter the new name. Select the option to Update references and click Finish.)
2.  Create a new public interface named BlitzController in the controller package. (Hint: to create an interface in Eclipse, right click on the package and choose New / Interface. Do not extend any other interfaces.)
    1.  Declare the following methods. No curly brackets should appear after the declaration, and no code should be provided to implement the method.)
        1.  Declare a public method named showBlitz(). It should take one parameter—a Player object named player—and return nothing.
        2.  Declare a public method named showDealDiscard(). It should take one parameter—a Card object named card—and return nothing.
        3.  Declare a public method named showDealer(). It should take one parameter—a Player object named dealer—and return nothing.
        4.  Declare a public method named showDiscard(). It should take three parameters—a Player object named player, a Card object named card, an integer named position—and return nothing.
        5.  Declare a public method named showDrawCard(). It should take two parameters—a Player object named player, a Card object named card—and return nothing.
        6.  Declare a public method named showEndGame(). It should take one parameter—a Player object named winner—and return nothing.
        7.  Declare a public method named showLoseTokens(). It should take two parameters—a Player object named player, an integer named count—and return nothing.
        8.  Declare a public method named showMyTurn(). It should take no parameters, and return nothing.
        9.  Declare a public method named showNewHand(). It should take no parameters, and return nothing.
        10.  Declare a public method named showRap(). It should take one parameter—a Player object named player—and return nothing.
        11.  Declare a public method named showTakeDiscard(). It should take three parameters—a Player object named player, a Card object named card, a Card object named nextDiscard—and return nothing.
        12.  Declare a public method named showUpdatedCards(). It should take one parameter—a Player object named player—and return nothing.

Run ItWhen you double click the exported JAR file name, the program should run with the same results as before.Key Points and More

*   Use an Interface to define required methods.
*   In the Blitz game, the BlitzController interface was defined with all the methods that the BlitzModel called on the controller.
*   The BlitzModel may then refer to the BlitzController interface instead of the BlitzControllerSwing class. In that way, the model will work with any controller class that implements the BlitzController interface.
*   To create another controller for a different view for the Blitz game, the controller must implement the BlitzController interface. To interact with the Blitz model, the controller must at some point call the following methods in BlitzModel:
    *   start() - to start the game. This method has no parameters.
    *   myPlayerDrewCard() - when the user performed an action on the view to draw a card. This method has no parameters.
    *   myPlayerTookDiscard() - when the user performed an action on the view to take the discard. This method has no parameters.
    *   myPlayerDiscarded() - when the user performed an action on the view to discard a card. This method has one parameter—the index of the card the user wants to discard.

I Hope You Enjoyed this BookI enjoy programming. As you've probably guessed, based on the kinds of programs I've put into my Do-It-Yourself Java Games books, I enjoy doing puzzles and playing games. To me, writing a computer game is like solving a puzzle. But as I work my way through these “puzzles,” I get to (have to) play the games I enjoy, giving me double the puzzle/game entertainment. Plus, I get to make the games work the way I want them to work. Therefore, for all these reasons, computer game programming is the ultimate puzzle for me. I hope writing these games has inspired you to try writing your own games, too.If you enjoyed this book:

In some cases, lessons specifically designed to teach these topics are found in the other Do-It-Yourself Java Games books.abstract classAn abstract class is a [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) that is intended for use only as a [superclass](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f2efb435a19e5114_10da2). [Objects](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_71c0aa408ef2c4da_10871) cannot be created from abstract classes.See [Key Points and More](#part0010.xhtml_anchor-0_1_4778c68fc4f07195_77dd) in [Lesson 5.2 - Create an Abstract Class](#part0010.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e3b9cdd721defea1_6a72).See [Key Points and More](#part0011.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1966537877e75b08_8f48) in [Lesson 6.1 - Use State-Driven Programming, Detect Collisions of Non-Rectangular Shapes](#part0011.xhtml_anchor-0_1_fa53d8bf72346ee2_7827).abstract methodAn abstract method is a [method](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c) with the abstract modifier and no [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f). Abstract methods must be declared within either an [abstract class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_43e3f7b067e9b9fb_f1a9) or an [interface](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d74c9b6cbdca9d02_10111). [Classes](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) that [extend](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1257f907c91f465_fb7e) an abstract class must provide code for all the abstract class's abstract methods.See [Key Points and More](#part0010.xhtml_anchor-0_1_4778c68fc4f07195_77dd) in [Lesson 5.2 - Create an Abstract Class](#part0010.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e3b9cdd721defea1_6a72).action listenerAction listeners are [classes](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) that [extend](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1257f907c91f465_fb7e) the [ActionListener](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7444464012a6c56c_f24f) class. They wait for [ActionEvents](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_963da834c79f1fe9_f20b).See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.7 - Buttons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.ActionEventAn ActionEvent is an [event](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_3922a8ab0211a33d_fa62) caused by the program [user](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f7ee8b295ae825fc_1104a) clicking a [button](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a7e3bb01f1245fef_f441), a [radio button](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_b056f4bd3bb27cb9_10a7f), a check box, or a [menu item](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_b7f6aa8fa05e49db_1060b), or by the [user](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f7ee8b295ae825fc_1104a) selecting an item from a list or pressing enter in a [text field](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e2690bf56590d934_10e7e). Add an [ActionListener](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7444464012a6c56c_f24f) to a [component](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685) to [run](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_33acc39cc7b992b0_10ba9) [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f) when an ActionEvent occurs.See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.7 - Buttons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.3 - Event Source in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Menu Bars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.ActionListenerAn ActionListener waits for an [ActionEvent](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_963da834c79f1fe9_f20b) from its assigned [component](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685). When an [ActionEvent](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_963da834c79f1fe9_f20b) occurs, Java [calls](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e67f7ce0908d82ce_f4f2) the ActionListener's actionPerformed() [method](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c).See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.7 - Buttons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Menu Bars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.alpha[Colors](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_9cc10cc4a245bbb3_f63b) can be created from four integer values: red, green, blue, and alpha. The alpha value, also known as the alpha channel, sets the transparency of a [color](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_9cc10cc4a245bbb3_f63b). The method may then use that value in its [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f).See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.1 - Methods with Parameters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.3 - Methods with Multiple Parameters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.ArithmeticExceptionAn ArithmeticException is an [exception](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_5826432d39c38488_fb22) thrown when a program attempts to do arithmetic that is not allowed, such as divide by zero.See Lesson 8.5 - Integer Subtraction, Multiplication, and Division in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.arrayAn array is one kind of Java list. [Elements](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_fdbf79bec1efa247_f9ea) of an array may be either Java [primitives](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a2edfb01eb7b5a61_109c5) or Java [Objects](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_71c0aa408ef2c4da_10871), but they must all have the same [type](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_883d6ce41c13bb5f_10ff1). The size of the array is set as part of the array [declaration](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_8f52562663593280_f878) and cannot be changed.See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.4 - Arrays in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 14.5 - Empty Array in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See [Key Points and More](#part0010.xhtml_anchor-0_1_58ddebf56fb69f6f_6a12) in [Lesson 5.1 - Use a Multi-Dimensional Array](#part0010.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a0b69e76a526902d_5ff0).ArrayListAn ArrayList is one kind of Java list. An ArrayList can only hold Java [Objects](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_71c0aa408ef2c4da_10871), not Java [primitives](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a2edfb01eb7b5a61_109c5), and all [elements](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_fdbf79bec1efa247_f9ea) in the list must have the same [type](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_883d6ce41c13bb5f_10ff1). The size of the ArrayList can be changed at any time by adding or removing elements.See Lesson 15.5 - Array Lists in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.audio fileAn audio file is a sound recording. To play a sound in Java, the audio file must be of type .wav or .au.See [Lesson 1.7 - Add Sound](#part0006.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a88dead359229963_fbe).AudioInputStreamAn AudioInputStream is an [InputStream](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_65ce2da9aafb6cfb_10054) formatted for audio input. Its data can be played back in real time, or put into a [Clip](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_48d29b42283f0a99_f5f0) to be played back later.See [Lesson 1.7 - Add Sound](#part0006.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a88dead359229963_fbe).background colorA [component](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685) is filled with its background color before its text or other details are added in the [foreground color](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1160bec8e8f12e5c_fdb8).See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.2 - Panels, Predefined Colors in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.block of codeA block of code is a group of zero or more lines of [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f), surrounded by curly brackets, { }.See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Classes, Superclasses and Programs in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.booleanBoolean is a basic data type. A boolean [variable](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1efec72ee65afe7_1105b) can have only two possible values, true or false. To specify a boolean value in a program, type “true” or “false”, but without the quotation marks.See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.5 - Boolean Data Type in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.BorderLayoutThe BorderLayout is a [layout](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_c1ec2d706f09968d_10446) best used whenever [components](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685) should be arranged in these five areas: across the top (PAGE_START), across the bottom (PAGE_END), along the left side between the top and bottom (LINE_START), along the right side between the top and bottom (LINE_END), and in the center (CENTER). Only one component is allowed in each of these areas. A component will be stretched to fill its assigned area.See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.1 - Border Layout in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.BoxLayoutThe BoxLayout is a [layout](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_c1ec2d706f09968d_10446) best used whenever any number of [components](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685) should be arranged in a row (X_AXIS) or in a column (Y_AXIS). When Java lays out components in a BoxLayout, components in a row layout might get stretched vertically and the components in a column layout might get stretched horizontally.See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.2 - Box Layout, Combined Layouts in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.breakA break [statement](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_4a3d3f8594048bd5_10cb8) may be used to break out of a [switch statement](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_c6fddee256a7d5b_10e2a) or a loop instead of [running](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_33acc39cc7b992b0_10ba9) the next line of [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f).See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.2 - Switch Statements in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.BufferedImageA BufferedImage is a Java [object](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_71c0aa408ef2c4da_10871) that allows access to image data. For example, individual pixels in the image may be changed.See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.2 - Read Image Files, Subimages, Image Icons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.4 - New Graphics, Scale an Image in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.1 - Transparent Colors, PNG Images in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.BufferedReaderA BufferedReader reads character data files more efficiently than [FileReaders](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_4c07cccdab23f2d3_fc42) or [InputStreamReaders](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_bd8d08a9e9f9e61d_10075). Therefore, [FileReaders](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_4c07cccdab23f2d3_fc42) and [InputStreamReaders](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_bd8d08a9e9f9e61d_10075) are typically used to create BufferedReaders, and then programs read file data using BufferedReaders.See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.2 - Read from a File, Catch Multiple Exceptions in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.7 - Put Data Files in the JAR File in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.BufferedWriterA BufferedWriter writes to character data files more efficiently than [FileWriters](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_ce6fe6f312927989_fc53). Therefore, FileWriters are typically used to create BufferedWriters, and then programs write file data using the BufferedWriter.See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.1 - Write to a File in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.build pathThe build path is a list of all the other [Java projects](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_cf63a8be27d3ec24_101b3) and [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f)-containing [libraries](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_3a080fa209b60d54_10483) that the current Java project needs to use.See Lesson 8.7 - Extend the DIYWindow Class in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See [Add a Project to the Build Path](#part0018.xhtml_anchor-0_1_5375a1e36d3865a_146c6) in [Appendix D - Using Eclipse](#part0018.xhtml).buttonA button usually refers to a [clickable](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_6414c477fad92f99_f5d8) [component](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685) in a [window](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_185c8a7e93daf2eb_1110e). When the component is clicked, an [ActionEvent](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_963da834c79f1fe9_f20b) is sent. If the program is listening for the [event](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_3922a8ab0211a33d_fa62), the program will usually respond in some way. Use the [JButton](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a51ccb175c0ff638_101d6) [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) to create a button or a [JRadioButton](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_18236a8dbe595115_102f5) to create a [radio button](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_b056f4bd3bb27cb9_10a7f).See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.7 - Buttons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.1 - A Custom Button, this in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 5.2 - In Focus Mark in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.1 - Buttons with Images in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.3 - Button Focus in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.2 - Text Fields, Radio Buttons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.6 - A Default Button in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.A button may also refer to one of the buttons on the mouse. For example, the left mouse button would be used for a left-click.See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.1 - Mouse Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.3 - Move Objects in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.button groupA button group is used to create a set of [radio buttons](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_b056f4bd3bb27cb9_10a7f). Only one [radio button](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_b056f4bd3bb27cb9_10a7f) in the group may be selected at a time. When a [radio button](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_b056f4bd3bb27cb9_10a7f) in the group is selected, the previously selected radio button will be deselected. Use the [ButtonGroup](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_79f984d021e78dc2_f4c7) [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) to create a button group.See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.2 - Text Fields, Radio Buttons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.ButtonGroupButtonGroup is the [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) used to [define](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1222d6b11f73bdf2_f8f2) a [button group](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_4bb308ced4b26edc_f4aa).See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.2 - Text Fields, Radio Buttons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.byteByte is a basic data type. A byte [variable](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1efec72ee65afe7_1105b) can hold [integers](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d0ddb62fa6bbd7f5_100e3) values between -128 and 127\. To specify a byte value in a program, type the value without the quotation marks.See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Integer Data Type and Addition in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.callWhen a [method](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c) is called, the program [runs](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_33acc39cc7b992b0_10ba9) the [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f) defined by that method before running the code that follows the method call.See Lesson 6.3 - Methods in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.caseA case label marks the start of the [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f) to be [run](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_33acc39cc7b992b0_10ba9) when a [switch statement](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_c6fddee256a7d5b_10e2a) expression evaluates to a value that matches the case value.See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.2 - Switch Statements in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.4 - Switch Default in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.6 - Case without Break in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 15.1 - Switch Statement with Integers in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.castCast converts an [object](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_71c0aa408ef2c4da_10871) of one [type](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_883d6ce41c13bb5f_10ff1) to another [type](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_883d6ce41c13bb5f_10ff1). A cast operation is indicated by putting a new [type](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_883d6ce41c13bb5f_10ff1) in parentheses before the name of a [variable](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1efec72ee65afe7_1105b) [defined](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1222d6b11f73bdf2_f8f2) with a different [type](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_883d6ce41c13bb5f_10ff1). The [variable's class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1efec72ee65afe7_1105b) must be a [superclass](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f2efb435a19e5114_10da2) of the [type](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_883d6ce41c13bb5f_10ff1) to which the object is being cast. If an [object](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_71c0aa408ef2c4da_10871) can't be cast to the new [type](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_883d6ce41c13bb5f_10ff1), a run time error will occur.See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.3 - Event Source in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.charA char is a Java [character](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f60e798719fa52c1_f57b) [variable](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1efec72ee65afe7_1105b).See Key Points and More in Lesson 15.2 - Character Data Type in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.characterCharacter is a basic data type, [declared](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_8f52562663593280_f878) in Java with “char”. A character [variable](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1efec72ee65afe7_1105b) can hold only a single [character](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f60e798719fa52c1_f57b) value. To specify a character value in a program, type the character surrounded with single quotation marks.See Key Points and More in Lesson 15.2 - Character Data Type in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.classA class is a blueprint from which [objects](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_71c0aa408ef2c4da_10871) are created. A class [defines](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1222d6b11f73bdf2_f8f2) the information the object can hold and the actions the object can take.See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Classes, Superclasses and Programs in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.7 - Extend the DIYWindow Class in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See [Create a First Program](#part0018.xhtml_anchor-0_1_eea89fcb904b339e_145ff) in [Appendix D - Using Eclipse](#part0018.xhtml).class variableA class variable has one copy of the [variable](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1efec72ee65afe7_1105b) shared by all [instances](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e84a0124fd42c25e_1008f) of its [declaring](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_8f52562663593280_f878) [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592). In contrast, each instance of a class has its own copy of an [instance variable](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_8e59a25ee8ca9e_100a9). A class variable may be used by any of the methods defined by that [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592), without the variable being [passed](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_837e620690c2ef56_1095e) to the methods as an [argument](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_99a431298dd48907_f2bd). Both class variables and instance variables must be declared in the class definition, not within class methods. Class variables must be declared with the [static](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_9407a2e934506325_10cee) modifier.clickableThis book refers to an [object](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_71c0aa408ef2c4da_10871) as clickable if clicking the mouse on the displayed representation of the object will result in the program taking an action.See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.1 - A Custom Button, this in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.1 - Mouse Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java GamesClipA clip is pre-loaded audio data, opened to an [AudioInputStream](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_51b9345396efc9dc_f347), that can be played back at a desired time.See [Key Points and More](#part0006.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d036dba4530febe3_121c) in [Lesson 1.7 - Add Sound](#part0006.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a88dead359229963_fbe).See [Lesson 6.1 - Use State-Driven Programming, Detect Collisions of Non-Rectangular Shapes](#part0011.xhtml_anchor-0_1_fa53d8bf72346ee2_7827).See [Lesson 7.4 - Use an Interface for State-Driven Design](#part0012_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_3f8e0064ae101500_a024).codeCode is a series of computer instructions that when [run](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_33acc39cc7b992b0_10ba9) in sequence perform a desired task.See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Classes, Superclasses and Programs in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.collision detectionCollision detection is the process of checking for intersection between two objects on the screen.See [Key Points and More](#part0009.xhtml_anchor-0_1_b42855ddd9a87628_5c6e) in [Lesson 4.2 - Detect Collisions of Rectangular Shapes](#part0009.xhtml_anchor-0_1_ab3302b3e7209667_51cc).See [Key Points and More](#part0011.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1966537877e75b08_8f48) in [Lesson 6.1 - Use State-Driven Programming, Detect Collisions of Non-Rectangular Shapes](#part0011.xhtml_anchor-0_1_fa53d8bf72346ee2_7827).colorColors are made up of a combination of red, green, and blue hues, and sometimes an [alpha](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_c689c0b597864d5b_f27f) value. The hue and alpha values each range from 0 through 255\. The higher the hue number, the more of that hue is in the color. Java provides predefined color [variables](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1efec72ee65afe7_1105b) for commonly used colors.See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.2 - Panels, Predefined Colors in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.6 - Custom Colors in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.1 - Transparent Colors, PNG Images in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.commentComments are notes put in [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f) to explain what the code is intended to do, or to label sections of code. Comments are ignored when the program is [run](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_33acc39cc7b992b0_10ba9). Comments are denoted by lines that begin with // or groups of lines that begin with /* and end with */.See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Comments in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.comment outYou can “comment out” lines of [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f) by turning those lines into a [comment](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_5d3020a98fc37ec0_f65d). When you turn code into a comment, that code will be ignored since programs ignore comments(comment).See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Comments in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.componentA component is any [window](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_185c8a7e93daf2eb_1110e) [object](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_71c0aa408ef2c4da_10871) that can be added to a Java [window](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_185c8a7e93daf2eb_1110e).See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Add Text, Window Size in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.2 - Panels, Predefined Colors in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.7 - Buttons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 3.1 - Text Areas in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 3.2 - Scroll Bars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.3 - Add and Remove Components in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Menu Bars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.2 - Text Fields, Radio Buttons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.3 - Space Between Components in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See [Key Points and More](#part0006.xhtml_anchor-0_1_578505eb0f9d4203_629) in [Lesson 1.1 - Create a Standard Project and Class](#part0006.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a3719cd6f765c4e7_4bd).component listenerComponent listeners are [classes](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) that [extend](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1257f907c91f465_fb7e) the [ComponentListener](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_9ffc0f07d7ce2309_f73e) [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592). They wait for [ComponentEvents](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a17199811c4c5ae_f721).See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.ComponentAdapterA ComponentAdapter is a [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) that eases [ComponentListener](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_9ffc0f07d7ce2309_f73e) [object](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_71c0aa408ef2c4da_10871) creation. Using a ComponentAdapter, a programmer writes [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f) only for the ComponentListener's [methods](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c) that will be used, rather than having to write code for all the methods [defined](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1222d6b11f73bdf2_f8f2) in ComponentListener. A ComponentAdapter may be used wherever a ComponentListener is required.See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.ComponentEventA ComponentEvent is an [event](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_3922a8ab0211a33d_fa62) caused by a [component](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685) changing size, location, or visibility. Add a [ComponentListener](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_9ffc0f07d7ce2309_f73e) or [ComponentAdapter](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7e79af9b53eace40_f701) to a component to run [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f) when the ComponentEvent occurs.See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.ComponentListenerA ComponentListener waits for a [ComponentEvent](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a17199811c4c5ae_f721) from its assigned [component](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685). When a ComponentEvent occurs, Java [calls](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e67f7ce0908d82ce_f4f2) the ComponentListener's componentHidden(), componentMoved(), componentResized(), or componentShown() [methods](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c).See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.confirm dialogA confirm dialog is a [dialog](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d50e18f9bae39dff_f933) that asks the [user](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f7ee8b295ae825fc_1104a) a question and waits for an answer. Though a confirm dialog can request other combinations of answers, this book uses confirm dialogs that expect only a yes or no answer. Use [JOptionPane](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a68fc136d13e5a81_102ae) to easily create a confirm dialog.See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.4 - Confirm Dialogs in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.consoleThe console displays Java error messages, or the program's System.out messages. In Eclipse, the console is usually displayed in the bottom pane of the [window](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_185c8a7e93daf2eb_1110e).See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.4 - Try/Catch Blocks and Exceptions in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.3 - Print to the Console in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.constructorA constructor is a special [method](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c) that is [called](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e67f7ce0908d82ce_f4f2) to create an [object](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_71c0aa408ef2c4da_10871) of that [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592).See Key Points and More in Lesson 16.2 - Constructors in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.containerA container is a [window](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_185c8a7e93daf2eb_1110e) [component](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685) that can hold more than one [component](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685), including other containers. [JFrame](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a2e632130691a36_10227) and [JPanel](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7741c4fb7a632007_102cc) are both container components.See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Add Text, Window Size in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.3 - Multiple Panels, Preferred Size, Dimension in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.controllerIn a [model/view/controller](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_4df0674422c946cc_106c8) design approach, the controller provides communication between the [model](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_bca0387e5a348c25_106a4) and the [view](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_9625e49bae9e0ad0_11070). The controller contains the [main()](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e7e1b0c0266556af_105af) [method](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e7e1b0c0266556af_105af) of the program, instructs the view about what to add or update in the display according to actions in the model, and sends [user](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f7ee8b295ae825fc_1104a) input from the view to the model.See [Key Points and More](#part0013_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_160b913137435593_c2e1) in [Lesson 8.1 - Lay out the Display in the “View”](#part0013_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_472610cf486ab292_b7e0).See [Key Points and More](#part0013_split_001.xhtml_anchor-0_1_34f7d8274f6c8efc_efc9) in [Lesson 8.4 - Set up Game Logic in the “Model”](#part0013_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_9090668e52edb67e_ce59).See [Key Points and More](#part0013_split_001.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d81848ff966b0cc6_f123) in [Lesson 8.5 - Reuse Game Logic](#part0013_split_001.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f9db5b5b34423341_f01b).coordinatesThe coordinates of a Java [object](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_71c0aa408ef2c4da_10871) refer to its location in a [container](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_b473cd3a3256c48c_f7a9), specified by a pair of x and y values. A location may identify the placement of a [window](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_185c8a7e93daf2eb_1110e) on the screen, or the placement of a [component](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685) within another component. The x value is the number of pixels to the left edge of the object from the left edge of its container, and the y value is the number of pixels to the top of the object from the top edge of its container.See Lesson 6.2 - Read Image Files, Subimages, Image Icons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.1 - A Painted Panel: Color, Rectangles, Lines, Circles, and Preferred Size in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.4 - New Graphics, Scale an Image in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.2 - Draw Strings, Font Metric in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.cursorThe mouse cursor is the symbol used to represent the location of the mouse pointer on the screen. When a new Date [object](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_71c0aa408ef2c4da_10871) is created with no [parameter](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_17ebea10ad901503_1092e) values, the Date object's time is set to the time maintained by the computer.See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.4 - Current Date, Date Format in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.DateFormatThe Java DateFormat [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) represents many different kinds of [date](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_994a7c06c504d776_f841) formats. DateFormat has [methods](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c) that are common to all date formats. However, to work with a date format [object](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_71c0aa408ef2c4da_10871), the program must first identify the [type](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_883d6ce41c13bb5f_10ff1) of the date format. A [SimpleDateFormat](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d7d72d5027a4d3c_10c30) is one kind of DateFormat.See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.4 - Current Date, Date Format in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.declareWhen you declare a [variable](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1efec72ee65afe7_1105b), you state that the variable exists, assign the variable's properties, and optionally assign to the variable an initial value. The declaration of a [method](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c) refers to the [statement](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_4a3d3f8594048bd5_10cb8) at the beginning of the method [definition](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1222d6b11f73bdf2_f8f2) that lists the method's properties, [return](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e35d24884a00e0a6_10b1a) [type](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_883d6ce41c13bb5f_10ff1), name, and [parameters](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_17ebea10ad901503_1092e).See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.3 - Variables, Strings, and the Escape Character in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.3 - Methods in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.1 - Methods with Parameters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.3 - Methods that Return a Value in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Static Methods in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.3 - Methods with Multiple Parameters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.default buttonThe default button means the same as the [default enter button](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_6985864ce9ef7041_f8cf).See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.6 - A Default Button in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.default enter buttonThe default enter button is the [button](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a7e3bb01f1245fef_f441) that will act as though it was clicked when someone presses the enter key, even when another [component](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685) in the [window](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_185c8a7e93daf2eb_1110e) has [focus](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c9719247172f865_fca3). For example, a window with [input fields](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1d57d3352d6c0067_10007) and a default enter button allows the program [user](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f7ee8b295ae825fc_1104a) to type in an input field and press the enter key to activate the [default button](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_ffbb4c96203c079b_f8be) without using the mouse.See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.6 - Message Dialogs in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.4 - Confirm Dialogs in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.2 - File Choosers in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.1 - A Custom Dialog in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.3 - Get Dialog Data in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.DimensionA Dimension is a [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) that holds two [integers](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d0ddb62fa6bbd7f5_100e3), usually representing width and height.See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.3 - Multiple Panels, Preferred Size, Dimension in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.disableIf a [component](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685) is disabled, it will no longer [listen](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_bd0561f4b8c8108a_1049e) for [events](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_3922a8ab0211a33d_fa62) or allow input.See Lesson 9.2 - Box Layout, Combined Layouts in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.doubleDouble is a basic data type. To specify a double value in a program, type the number including a decimal point but no quotation marks.See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.6 - Double Data Type in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.double bufferAnimation is smoother if drawings are double buffered: first draw on an off-screen image, then paint the image to the screen.
