Refer to a specific element in an array or ArrayList by giving its [index](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_8d3f180dcf05865a_ff9f), its position in the array or ArrayList.See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.4 - Arrays in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 14.5 - Empty Array in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Lesson 15.6 - Array Lists in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.ellipsisAn ellipsis is a series of three dots, …, usually used to indicate that some information has been omitted.See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.3 - Font in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.Ellipses are used in the [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f) [listings](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_8f65caac9a11e926_10538) in this book to represent lines of code that are not shown.else blockAn else block is an optional [block of code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_87fccad38ae0c449_f36e) added to the end of an [if statement](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d4c8c577a58feec1_fe80). The else block [runs](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_33acc39cc7b992b0_10ba9) only if the [if statement](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d4c8c577a58feec1_fe80) test evaluates to false.See Key Points and More in Lesson 5.1 - If Statements, Strings that are Equal or Contain Letters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.enableIf a [component](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685) is enabled, it will [listen](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_bd0561f4b8c8108a_1049e) for [events](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_3922a8ab0211a33d_fa62) and allow input.See Lesson 9.2 - Box Layout, Combined Layouts in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.escape characterThe escape character (backslash, \,) is used to mark special characters in a [string](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_636f36eeb6f3b8f0_10d22).See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.4 - Joining Strings, the Escape Character in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.eventAn event is used to indicate that an action was taken on a [component](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685), usually by a program [user](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f7ee8b295ae825fc_1104a). Examples of events are a mouse clicked, a key pressed, a [button](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a7e3bb01f1245fef_f441) clicked, or a [window](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_185c8a7e93daf2eb_1110e) resized.See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.7 - Buttons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.3 - Event Source in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.2 - Key Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.1 - Mouse Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.3 - Focus Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Draw with a Mouse, Mouse Motion Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.event dispatch threadAll Swing [window](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_185c8a7e93daf2eb_1110e) [events](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_3922a8ab0211a33d_fa62), such as mouse clicks, [keyboard input](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_ff1594eace1e8479_103b9), [component](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685) [repaint](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_b370d9d07ee4e9ed_10a9c), and more are performed on a separate [thread](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_2a0963431d6e1d34_10ea3), called the event dispatch thread, also referred to as the [EDT](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_8db8b6a1f1e82544_f9ae).See [Key Points and More](#part0006.xhtml_anchor-0_1_578505eb0f9d4203_629) in [Lesson 1.1 - Create a Standard Project and Class](#part0006.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a3719cd6f765c4e7_4bd).See [Key Points and More](#part0006.xhtml_anchor-0_1_cca9f924d165cb5_b87) in [Lesson 1.5 - Create a Thread](#part0006.xhtml_anchor-0_1_8d852bced73c109_afb).See [Key Points and More](#part0006.xhtml_anchor-0_1_b217ba14343b6cb3_f9b) in [Lesson 1.6 - Stop a Thread](#part0006.xhtml_anchor-0_1_4d6fc544802f1a5a_c23).See [Key Points and More](#part0008.xhtml_anchor-0_1_61614548c2a13f76_4152) in [Lesson 3.2 - Pause the Event Dispatch Thread](#part0008.xhtml_anchor-0_1_71c56116e9af500_3bb4).See [Key Points and More](#part0013_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_591f5ef148bde4bb_c886) in [Lesson 8.2 - Stop All Activity with a Sleeping Thread](#part0013_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_83ab6d7df4fe020_c2f6).event-driven programmingEvent-driven programming is a style of programming in which the program sets up the desired environment, then just waits for [events](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_3922a8ab0211a33d_fa62). The program then responds to the events as they occur, in whatever order they happen.See the Introduction in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.event queueJava's event queue is a list used as a control mechanism for handling [events](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_3922a8ab0211a33d_fa62) from a [window's](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_185c8a7e93daf2eb_1110e) many different inputs. All Swing [components](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685) use the event queue for handling events. Components created in the [main()](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e7e1b0c0266556af_105af) [method](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e7e1b0c0266556af_105af) require [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f) to add the component to the event queue.See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.9 - Event Queue in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.exceptionAn exception is an event that occurs while running [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f), disrupting the code's usual execution flow. For example, an exception will occur if s program tries to convert a [string](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_636f36eeb6f3b8f0_10d22) with alphabetic characters into an [integer](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d0ddb62fa6bbd7f5_100e3), or if a program tries to read from a file that does not exist. The program should include [try/catch blocks](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_c3929929bb8b579b_10fcd) containing code for handling anticipated exception occurrences.See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.4 - Try/Catch Blocks and Exceptions in Do-It-Yourself Java Games in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See [Key Points and More](#part0012_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_38ab58201d404b72_9cb7) in [Lesson 7.2 - Create and Throw Custom Exceptions](#part0012_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_56f1af00984edb6c_94c3).exit codeAn exit code is an [integer](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d0ddb62fa6bbd7f5_100e3) used with System's exit() [method](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c), indicating whether the program exited as expected.See [Key Points and More](#part0012_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_62459d8cfacdef4f_94a2) in [Lesson 7.1 - Use System Exit Codes](#part0012_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_6c423710e7c6711e_8f99).exportExporting a program takes the program out of Eclipse and puts it in a separate [JAR file](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_5d5d59d7dce4a8ac_10191). The program can then be [run](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_33acc39cc7b992b0_10ba9) without Eclipse.See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.2 - Export a Program in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See [Export a Program](#part0018.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1d33694d7bf09214_1470a) in [Appendix D - Using Eclipse](#part0018.xhtml).extendA [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) may already exist that provides functionality close to that needed for a new class. Instead of adding more [variables](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1efec72ee65afe7_1105b) and [methods](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c) to the first [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592), and instead of repeating all the first class's variables and methods in the new class, [define](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1222d6b11f73bdf2_f8f2) the new class to extend the first class. The original class then serves as the [superclass](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f2efb435a19e5114_10da2) of the new class.See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.7 - Extend the DIYWindow Class in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.extractExtracting files is the process of copying and decompressing files from a [ZIP file](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_ab33a1e023f7b50c_11235) or [JAR file](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_5d5d59d7dce4a8ac_10191) into another folder on the computer.See [Download and Install Eclipse](#part0017.xhtml_anchor-0_1_675f74414f058471_14479) in [Appendix C - Setup](#part0017.xhtml).See [Download AdvancedDIYJava.zip Detailed Instructions](#part0017.xhtml_anchor-0_1_41ff82e7d2329e50_144c5) in [Appendix C - Setup](#part0017.xhtml).FileThe Java File [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) allows programs to work with the contents of a file and the file's path name.See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.2 - Read Image Files, Subimages, Image Icons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.2 - File Choosers in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Lesson 9.2 - Box Layout, Combined Layouts in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See [Key Points and More](#part0006.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d036dba4530febe3_121c)  in [Lesson 1.7 - Add Sound](#part0006.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a88dead359229963_fbe).See [Lesson 2.1 - Drag Objects, Use a Dictionary](#part0007.xhtml_anchor-0_1_de184c329bfa417a_12ab).file chooserA file chooser is a [dialog](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d50e18f9bae39dff_f933) that allows the [user](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f7ee8b295ae825fc_1104a) to browse through a list of files on his computer and choose a file to use in the program. Create a file chooser using [JFileChooser](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_3c1f8648f379d5b2_10213).See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.2 - File Choosers in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.file filterA file filter applied to a [file chooser](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f89fc06f32e2cf8a_fbec) will restrict the files in the chooser's list by some criteria. For example, a file filter could be added to include only those files with a specific file name extension. Create a file filter using the [FileFilter](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_8dd683da65fc7c04_fc17) class.See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.3 - An Image File Filter in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.FileFilterFileFilter is the [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) that should be [extended](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1257f907c91f465_fb7e) to create a [file filter](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f71790ce4dcf2228_fc03).See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.3 - An Image File Filter in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.FileNotFoundExceptionA FileNotFoundException is an [exception](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_5826432d39c38488_fb22) [thrown](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7af6f0b4fdec3e27_10f0a) when a program tries to read from a file that does not exist.See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.2 - Read from a File, Catch Multiple Exceptions in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.FileReaderA FileReader reads [character](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f60e798719fa52c1_f57b) data from a file.See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.2 - Read from a File, Catch Multiple Exceptions in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.FileWriterA FileWriter writes character data to a file.See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.1 - Write to a File in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.finalThe value of a [variable](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1efec72ee65afe7_1105b) [declared](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_8f52562663593280_f878) with the [final](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_bb9cd4ac30b08075_fc61) attribute is set and then never again changed by the program.See Key Points and More in Lesson 14.6 - Static Final Variables in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.floatFloat is a basic data type in Java. A float [variable](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1efec72ee65afe7_1105b) can hold a decimal number with as many as 7 decimal places. To specify a float value in a program, type the value with a decimal point, add an “f” to the end of the value, and use no quotation marks.See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.6 - Double Data Type in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.FlowLayoutThe FlowLayout is a [layout](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_c1ec2d706f09968d_10446) best used whenever any number of [components](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685) should be arranged in a row, and each displayed at its [preferred size](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e9343816b6879acf_1099e). However, additional rows will be created in a FlowLayout if not all the components fit within the width of the [container](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_b473cd3a3256c48c_f7a9).See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.3 - Multiple Panels, Preferred Size, Dimension in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.focusThe [component](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685) in focus will receive [keyboard input](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_ff1594eace1e8479_103b9). Only one component will be in focus at a time. Focus is often referred to as keyboard focus.See Key Points and More in Lesson 5.2 - In Focus Mark in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.3 - Button Focus in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.3 - Focus Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.focus listenerFocus listeners are [classes](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) that [extend](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1257f907c91f465_fb7e) the [FocusListener](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f326191781a7f0f_fd39) class. They wait for [FocusEvents](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_716bdcdbae20bf43_fd19).See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.3 - Focus Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.focus markFocus mark refers to the mark that gets painted on a [component](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685) when the component is in [focus](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c9719247172f865_fca3). For example, a [button](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a7e3bb01f1245fef_f441) will have a rectangle painted around the button's text when the button is in [focus](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c9719247172f865_fca3).See Key Points and More in Lesson 5.2 - In Focus Mark in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.FocusAdapterA FocusAdapter is a [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) that eases [FocusListener](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f326191781a7f0f_fd39) [object](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_71c0aa408ef2c4da_10871) creation. Using a FocusAdapter, a programmer writes [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f) only for the FocusListener's [methods](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c) that will be used, rather than having to write code for all the [defined](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1222d6b11f73bdf2_f8f2) FocusListener methods. A FocusAdapter may be used wherever a FocusListener is required.See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.3 - Focus Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.FocusEventA FocusEvent is an [event](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_3922a8ab0211a33d_fa62) caused by a [component](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685) coming into [focus](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c9719247172f865_fca3) or going out of focus. Add a [FocusListener](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f326191781a7f0f_fd39) to a component to [run](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_33acc39cc7b992b0_10ba9) [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f) when the FocusEvent occurs.See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.3 - Focus Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.FocusListenerA FocusListener waits for a [FocusEvent](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_716bdcdbae20bf43_fd19) from its assigned [component](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685). When a FocusEvent occurs, Java [calls](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e67f7ce0908d82ce_f4f2) the FocusListener's focusGained() or focusLost() [method](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c).See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.3 - Focus Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.fontA font [defines](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1222d6b11f73bdf2_f8f2) how characters will be drawn to the display. A font defines the type design, style, and size of the characters.See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.3 - Font in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.2 - Draw Strings, Font Metrics in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.font metricsFont metrics are the measurements of how text is rendered in a specific [font](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d3af6dcbb29e4420_fd57). A font metrics [object](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_71c0aa408ef2c4da_10871) can calculate the measurements of text, or of portions of character symbols. Use [FontMetrics](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_3121db22c1265a38_fd86) to create font metrics.See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.2 - Draw Strings, Font Metrics in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.FontMetricsFontMetrics is the [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) used to create a [font metrics](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_9d4674c43d54a227_fd6f) [object](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_71c0aa408ef2c4da_10871).See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.2 - Draw Strings, Font Metrics in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.for loopA for loop is a [block of code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_87fccad38ae0c449_f36e) that repeats a set number of times. A for loop typically [initializes](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_302a59a80b054076_ffd9) an iteration [variable](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1efec72ee65afe7_1105b), increments or decrements the iteration variable, and terminates when the iteration variable reaches a particular value.See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.1 - For Loops in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.foreground colorThe foreground color is the [color](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_9cc10cc4a245bbb3_f63b) used for the text or symbols that are drawn onto a [component](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685). For example, the circle for a [radio button](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_b056f4bd3bb27cb9_10a7f) will be drawn using the foreground color.See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.4 - Foreground Color in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.glue componentGlue components are often added to a [container](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_b473cd3a3256c48c_f7a9) using [BoxLayout](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_6eecab2ef493de1c_f3a4) to add space between other [components](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685). Glue components are invisible and all glue components in a container will stretch in size equally to use up any extra space in that row or column. To add an exact amount of space that won't stretch, use a [rigid component](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_fe6fa91ddd194c28_10b55) instead.See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.3 - Space Between Components in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.graphical user interfaceA graphical user interface, often abbreviated as [GUI](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a9fd30372fa5ac2_fe49), is a visual way for program [users](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f7ee8b295ae825fc_1104a) to interact with a computer. A [GUI](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a9fd30372fa5ac2_fe49) consists of a [window](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_185c8a7e93daf2eb_1110e), plus [buttons](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a7e3bb01f1245fef_f441), menus, and any other visual input methods that allow a [user](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f7ee8b295ae825fc_1104a) to express what he wants the program to do.See Lesson 2.1 - Border Layout in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.GraphicsThe Graphics [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) allows a program to draw, scale, or rotate the contents of an image, or to draw on a [component](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685).See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.1 - A Painted Panel: Color, Rectangles, Lines, Circles, and Preferred Size in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.4 - New Graphics, Scale an Image in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.2 - Draw Strings, Font Metrics in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.4 - XOR Mode in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.GridLayoutThe GridLayout is a [layout](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_c1ec2d706f09968d_10446) best used whenever [components](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685) should be arranged in a grid, with each section the same size. If components are not all the same size, they will be stretched so they are displayed the same size.See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.2 - Grid Layout in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.GUIGUI stands for [Graphical User Interface](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_cf298a95114c3394_fdee).See Lesson 2.1 - Border Layout in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.horizontal alignmentUse a [label's](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_404728b6c38127f6_1042b) setHorizontalAlignment0 [method](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c) to horizontally align text in a [label](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_404728b6c38127f6_1042b). Use a [container's](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_b473cd3a3256c48c_f7a9) setAlignmentX() method to horizontally align a [component](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685) in its container.See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.4 - Align Text in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.2 - Box Layout, Combined Layouts in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.if statementAn if [statement](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_4a3d3f8594048bd5_10cb8) is a [block of code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_87fccad38ae0c449_f36e) that [runs](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_33acc39cc7b992b0_10ba9) only if the specified test evaluates to true. An if statement may also have an optional [else block](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a665a5a5461c94c_fa22) that runs only if the test evaluates to false.See Key Points and More in Lesson 5.1 - If Statements, Strings that are Equal or Contain Letters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.ImageThe Image [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) represents many different kinds of images. Image provides [methods](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c) that are common to all images. However, Image is an [abstract class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_43e3f7b067e9b9fb_f1a9). To create an Image, a program must use one of Image's subclasses. A [BufferedImage](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_49ddcaa2c6005877_f3d2) is a subclass of Image.See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.2 - Read Image Files, Subimages, Image Icons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.4 - New Graphics, Scale an Image in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.2 - Save an Image in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.image buttonAn image button is a [button](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a7e3bb01f1245fef_f441) that displays an image instead of text. Create an image button using [JButton](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a51ccb175c0ff638_101d6) and an [ImageIcon](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_93e245fe717229a0_fef7).See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.1 - Buttons with Images in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.image labelAn image label is a [label](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_404728b6c38127f6_1042b) that displays an image instead of text. Create an image label using [JLabel](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_4a3a569a571bde6d_10257) and an [ImageIcon](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_93e245fe717229a0_fef7).See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.ImageIconAn ImageIcon [object](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_71c0aa408ef2c4da_10871) is typically a small image and is easily loaded into the program using the file name or URL. ImageIcons are often used for images on [buttons](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a7e3bb01f1245fef_f441) and in [labels](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_404728b6c38127f6_1042b). An ImageIcon is not a subclass of [Image](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_8e0e9e83acafd60e_fe9a), so an ImageIcon may not be used where [Images](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_8e0e9e83acafd60e_fe9a) are expected, nor may an [Image](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_8e0e9e83acafd60e_fe9a) be used where an ImageIcon is expected.See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.1 - Buttons with Images in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.2 - Read Image Files, Subimages, Image Icons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.2 - Save an Image in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.ImageIOImageIO is a [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) used for reading and writing image files of various types.See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.2 - Read Image Files, Subimages, Image Icons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.2 - Save an Image in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.1 - Transparent Colors, PNG Images in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.implementJava [interfaces](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d74c9b6cbdca9d02_10111) are associated with a [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) by including the key word implements in the class's declaration. When a class implements an interface, it must provide [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f) for all methods [declared](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_8f52562663593280_f878) in the interface.See [Key Points and More](#part0006.xhtml_anchor-0_1_cca9f924d165cb5_b87) in [Lesson 1.5 - Create a Thread](#part0006.xhtml_anchor-0_1_8d852bced73c109_afb).See [Key Points and More](#part0008.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7130df9394b0c4e2_49a2) in [Lesson 3.3 - Define a Thread Inline](#part0008.xhtml_anchor-0_1_639dcd699dd1c581_419c).See [Key Points and More](#part0012_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_31c9bd10d2a7d268_9fcc) in [Lesson 7.3 - Create an Interface](#part0012_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_b65c95057539c6d8_9d1e).See [Key Points and More](#part0013_split_001.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d81848ff966b0cc6_f123) in [Lesson 8.5 - Reuse Game Logic](#part0013_split_001.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f9db5b5b34423341_f01b).importJava must have the full, proper name of every [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) it uses in a program, including the class's [package](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_933bf66eb34c8a11_108eb) name. Use import [statements](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_4a3d3f8594048bd5_10cb8) in a class definition to provide the full name of the classes it uses, so the class may refer to those imported classes by name only, without their package names. Import a class by adding an import statement for that class at the beginning of the class [definition](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1222d6b11f73bdf2_f8f2). Import statements are not needed for classes defined in the java.lang package.See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.2 - Generate Random Numbers in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.indexAn index is the position of an item in an ordered collection of items. For example, indexes are used to name the position of a [character](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f60e798719fa52c1_f57b) in a [string](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_636f36eeb6f3b8f0_10d22), or an [element](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_fdbf79bec1efa247_f9ea) in an [array](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_59e210b3f891158a_f2f3). The [iteration variable](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e6689e84bb0eccf0_10174) in a [for](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_bf1812ac796a1473_fd9d) [loop](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_bf1812ac796a1473_fd9d) is also sometimes referred to as the loop index.See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.4 - Index of Characters in a String in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 15.3 - Index of Next Character in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.infinite loopAn infinite loop is a [block of code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_87fccad38ae0c449_f36e) that would repeat forever because an end condition is never met. You may have to use the Eclipse terminate button, or reboot the computer, to end an infinite loop.See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.3 - Infinite Loops in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.initializeTo initialize a [variable](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1efec72ee65afe7_1105b), assign its first value.See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.3 - Variables, Strings, and the Escape Character in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.inline[Classes](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) may be [defined](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1222d6b11f73bdf2_f8f2) inline, meaning the class is defined within the [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f) of the definition of another class. If the class that is being defined inline is not assigned to a [variable](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1efec72ee65afe7_1105b), it is called an anonymous inline definition. A class defined inline is sometimes referred to as an inner class.See [Key Points and More](#part0008.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7130df9394b0c4e2_49a2) in [Lesson 3.3 - Define a Thread Inline](#part0008.xhtml_anchor-0_1_639dcd699dd1c581_419c).input fieldAn input field is a [component](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685) that allows a program [user](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f7ee8b295ae825fc_1104a) to enter character data to be used by a program. Create an input stream using [InputStream](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_65ce2da9aafb6cfb_10054).See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.7 - Put Data Files in the JAR File in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See [Key Points and More](#part0006.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d036dba4530febe3_121c) in [Lesson 1.7 - Add Sound](#part0006.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a88dead359229963_fbe).InputStreamThe InputStream [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) is used to create an [input stream](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_602bb08ce0f123d6_10036) of [non-character data](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_b63c71b8fe8faeb6_10829).See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.7 - Put Data Files in the JAR File in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See [Key Points and More](#part0006.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d036dba4530febe3_121c) in [Lesson 1.7 - Add Sound](#part0006.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a88dead359229963_fbe).InputStreamReaderThe InputStreamReader [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) is used to read [non-character data](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_b63c71b8fe8faeb6_10829) from an [input stream](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_602bb08ce0f123d6_10036) and convert it into [character](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f60e798719fa52c1_f57b) data.See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.7 - Put Data Files in the JAR File in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.instanceA [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) is a [definition](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1222d6b11f73bdf2_f8f2) of an [object](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_71c0aa408ef2c4da_10871). An object, or [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) instance, is created from a class definition.See Key Points and More in Lesson 16.1 - Objects, Card in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.instance variableAn instance variable is a [variable](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1efec72ee65afe7_1105b) [declared](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_8f52562663593280_f878) in a [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) [definition](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1222d6b11f73bdf2_f8f2) instead of in a [method](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c). Such a variable may be used by any of the methods defined by that [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592), without the variable being [passed](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_837e620690c2ef56_1095e) to the methods as an [argument](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_99a431298dd48907_f2bd). Each object created from the class has its own copy of the instance variable.See Key Points and More in Lesson 14.3 - Instance Variables in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.intInt is a basic data type in Java. An int [variable](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1efec72ee65afe7_1105b) can hold an [integer](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d0ddb62fa6bbd7f5_100e3) value between -2,147,483,648 and 2,147,483,647\. To specify an int value in a program, type the value without quotation marks.See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Integer Data Type and Addition in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.integerAn integer is a whole number value, either positive or negative. An integer value is typed without quotation marks and without a decimal point. Integer [variables](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1efec72ee65afe7_1105b) are [declared](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_8f52562663593280_f878) in Java as “[int](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_92b7614274f15d5e_100cf)”, “[byte](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_fe763560a9de37c_f4de)”, “[short](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f2111e4ae8f7461f_10c19)”, or “[long](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_9e655349e5fdc8e3_1058a)”.See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Integer Data Type and Addition in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.2 - Convert a String to an Integer in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.5 - Integer Subtraction, Multiplication, and Division in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.interfaceAn interface is a Java construct containing only [method](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c) [declarations](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_8f52562663593280_f878) and [final](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_bb9cd4ac30b08075_fc61) [static](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_9407a2e934506325_10cee) [variables](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1efec72ee65afe7_1105b). All declared methods will be required to be [defined](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1222d6b11f73bdf2_f8f2) in any [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) that [implements](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_5f1e072a6ae679dc_ff4b) the interface. Starting with Java 8, interfaces may also include fully defined static methods and fully defined default methods. Interface default methods are not used in this book.See [Key Points and More](#part0006.xhtml_anchor-0_1_cca9f924d165cb5_b87) in [Lesson 1.5 - Create a Thread](#part0006.xhtml_anchor-0_1_8d852bced73c109_afb).See [Key Points and More](#part0012_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_31c9bd10d2a7d268_9fcc) in  [Lesson 7.3 - Create an Interface](#part0012_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_b65c95057539c6d8_9d1e).See [Key Points and More](#part0012_split_001.xhtml_anchor-0_1_3abf22024cff18fa_b75f) in [Lesson 7.4 - Use an Interface for State-Driven Design](#part0012_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_3f8e0064ae101500_a024).See [Key Points and More](#part0013_split_001.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d81848ff966b0cc6_f123) in [Lesson 8.5 - Reuse Game Logic](#part0013_split_001.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f9db5b5b34423341_f01b).IOExceptionAn IOException is an [exception](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_5826432d39c38488_fb22) [thrown](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7af6f0b4fdec3e27_10f0a) when an error occurs as a program tries to read from or write to a file. For example, the IOException is thrown if a file that exists can't be opened.See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.1 - Write to a File in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.2 - Read from a File, Catch Multiple Exceptions in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.iteration variableAn iteration variable is a [variable](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1efec72ee65afe7_1105b) [declared](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_8f52562663593280_f878) in a [for loop](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_bf1812ac796a1473_fd9d), incremented or decremented each time through the loop, and compared against another value as a loop exit test. The iteration variable, sometimes also called the loop [index](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_8d3f180dcf05865a_ff9f) or loop control variable, is used to control the number of times a [for loop](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_bf1812ac796a1473_fd9d) runs.See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.1 - For Loops in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.JAR fileA JAR file is a Java Archive file. It contains one or more folders or files of Java [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f). A JAR file is named with “.jar” as its extension. If a JAR file is created as a Java executable file, the program in the JAR file can be [run](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_33acc39cc7b992b0_10ba9) by simply double-clicking on the name of the JAR file.See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.1 - Java Projects and Packages in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.2 - Export a Program in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.7 - Put Data Files in the JAR File in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.Java projectA Java project is the highest level of organization of Java [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f) in Eclipse. Each program in this book is organized as a separate Java project in Eclipse. A Java project contains one or more [packages](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_933bf66eb34c8a11_108eb), and each package contains one or more [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) [definitions](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1222d6b11f73bdf2_f8f2). Most of the Java projects in this book contain only one package because these programs are relatively small.See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.1 - Java Projects and Packages in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See [Create a First Project](#part0018.xhtml_anchor-0_1_778d8345f5364637_14540) in [Appendix D - Buttons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.1 - A Custom Button, this in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 5.1 - Another Custom Button in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.1 - Add Text, Window Size in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.JMenuJMenu is the [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) used to create a [menu](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_effccf0fec923ae6_105dd).See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Menu Bars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.JMenuBarJMenuBar is the [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) used to create a [menu bar](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_6bd486b000c0e5bf_105f4).See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Menu Bars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.JMenuItemJMenuItem is the [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) used to create a [menu item](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_b7f6aa8fa05e49db_1060b).See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Menu Bars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.JOptionPaneJOptionPane is the [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) that eases displaying a [message dialog](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_b78b46ccaf904d59_1062b) or a [confirm dialog](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f0afcc43f083a5b3_f760).See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.8 - Panels, Predefined Colors in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.JPEGJPEG is a format for image files. JPEG stands for Joint Photographic Experts Group.
