JTextAreas are usually used as [input fields](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1d57d3352d6c0067_10007).See Key Points and More in Lesson 3.1 - Text Areas in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.JTextFieldJTextField is the [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) used to create a text [input field](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1d57d3352d6c0067_10007).See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.2 - Text Fields, Radio Buttons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.JToolBarJToolBar is the [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) used to create a [toolbar](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_313b277f9643eb_10f90).See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.key codeA key code of a [KeyEvent](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a3b49ebe83621b3a_103da) is a number that represents the keyboard key that was pressed. Key codes are [static](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_9407a2e934506325_10cee) [integer](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d0ddb62fa6bbd7f5_100e3) [variables](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1efec72ee65afe7_1105b) whose name starts with VK_. A key code represents which key was pressed, not the [character](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f60e798719fa52c1_f57b) value of that key. VK stands for virtual key.See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.2 - Key Listener in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.key listenerA key listeners is a [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) that [extends](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1257f907c91f465_fb7e) the [KeyListener](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7e944c9abc5802d1_103fa) class. A key listener waits for [KeyEvents](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a3b49ebe83621b3a_103da).See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.2 - Key Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.KeyAdapterA KeyAdapter is a [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) that eases [KeyListener](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7e944c9abc5802d1_103fa) [object](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_71c0aa408ef2c4da_10871) creation. Using a KeyAdapter, a programmer writes [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f) only for the [KeyListener's](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7e944c9abc5802d1_103fa) [methods](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c) that will be used, rather than having to write code for all the methods [defined](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1222d6b11f73bdf2_f8f2) in KeyListener. A KeyAdapter may be used wherever a [KeyListener](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7e944c9abc5802d1_103fa) is required.See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.2 - Key Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.keyboard inputKeyboard input refers to data that comes to a program as a result of a [user](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f7ee8b295ae825fc_1104a) pressing keys on a keyboard. [Input fields](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1d57d3352d6c0067_10007) could be used to receive keyboard input. Or a [key listener](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e6300aa859686c17_10379) could be created to [listen](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_bd0561f4b8c8108a_1049e) for keyboard input.See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.2 - Key Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.2 - Text Fields, Radio Buttons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.KeyEventA KeyEvent is an [event](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_3922a8ab0211a33d_fa62) caused by a program [user](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f7ee8b295ae825fc_1104a) pressing a key on a keyboard. Add a [KeyListener](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7e944c9abc5802d1_103fa) to a [component](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685) to [run](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_33acc39cc7b992b0_10ba9) [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f) when the KeyEvent occurs.See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.2 - Key Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.KeyListenerA KeyListener waits for a [KeyEvent](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a3b49ebe83621b3a_103da) from its assigned [component](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685). When a KeyEvent occurs, Java [calls](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e67f7ce0908d82ce_f4f2) the KeyListener's keyPressed(), keyReleased(), or keyTyped() [method](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c).See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.2 - Key Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.keystrokeA keystroke is the act of pressing a keyboard key. Programs can process data about a keystroke that includes any modifiers added to the key, such as Alt, Ctrl, Shift, or mouse [button](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a7e3bb01f1245fef_f441) down.See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.2 - Key Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.labelA label usually consists of a single line of text displayed in a [container](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_b473cd3a3256c48c_f7a9). However, an image or a combination of an image and text can also serve as a label. Create a label using [JLabel](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_4a3a569a571bde6d_10257).See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Add Text, Window Size in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.layoutA [container's](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_b473cd3a3256c48c_f7a9) layout [defines](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1222d6b11f73bdf2_f8f2) how [components](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685) will be arranged in the container. Java calculates the best fit, considering each component's size, the layout chosen, and the system's defined [look and feel](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_5c2c632906a71978_1059e). Layouts explained in the book More Do-It-Yourself Java Games include [BorderLayout](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1257a735c16bfdeb_f390), [BoxLayout](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_6eecab2ef493de1c_f3a4), [FlowLayout](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_9a570b66d48d1e62_fc89), and [GridLayout](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f03ba22a2b46129_fe35).See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.1 - Border Layout in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.3 - Multiple Panels, Preferred Size, Dimension in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.2 - Grid Layout in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.2 - Box Layout, Combined Layouts in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.libraryEclipse refers to an external [JAR file](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_5d5d59d7dce4a8ac_10191) as a library. For example, DIYJava.jar is a [JAR file](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_5d5d59d7dce4a8ac_10191) that must be added as a library in the [build path](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_16ade889aa555e58_f423) of any [Java project](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_cf63a8be27d3ec24_101b3) that uses the DIYWindow [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592).See Lesson 1.1 - Java Projects and Packages in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.listen[Code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f) listens for a [user](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f7ee8b295ae825fc_1104a) action on a [component](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685), waiting for a specific kind of [event](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_3922a8ab0211a33d_fa62). Each type of user action requires a different type of [listener](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1544cc5956846959_104e5).See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.7 - Buttons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.3 - Event Source in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.2 - Key Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.1 - Mouse Listener in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.5 - Component Listener, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.3 - Focus Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Draw with a Mouse, Mouse Motion Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.listenerA listener is [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f) written to [listen](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_bd0561f4b8c8108a_1049e) for [events](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_3922a8ab0211a33d_fa62). Different kinds of events, such as when a program [user](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f7ee8b295ae825fc_1104a) clicks a mouse [button](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a7e3bb01f1245fef_f441), may be recognized by a different type of listener, such as a [mouse listener](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_c0392751225e8a1b_10710). Each [type](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_883d6ce41c13bb5f_10ff1) of listener, such as a [MouseListener](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_6b130b8c6b00e752_107c0), is [defined](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1222d6b11f73bdf2_f8f2) in a separate class. Each class provides different [methods](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c) for processing an event, such as mousePressed() or mouseReleased().See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.7 - Buttons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.2 - Key Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.1 - Mouse Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.3 - Focus Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Draw with a Mouse, Mouse Motion Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.listingA program listing usually shows all the [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f) for that program. The listings in this book are only partial listings. They use an [ellipsis](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1381e0db215681e_fa0d), …, to indicate where code from the program is not shown.See Lesson 1.2 - Classes, Superclasses and Programs in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See [Appendix B - Completed Listings](#part0016_split_000.xhtml).logicProgram logic refers to how program [objects](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_71c0aa408ef2c4da_10871) interact to enable a program to accomplish its intent. This program logic is also sometimes referred to more specifically to its purpose as game logic, domain logic, or business logic.See [Key Points and More](#part0013_split_001.xhtml_anchor-0_1_34f7d8274f6c8efc_efc9) in [Lesson 8.4 - Set up Game Logic in the “Model”](#part0013_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_9090668e52edb67e_ce59).See [Key Points and More](#part0013_split_001.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d81848ff966b0cc6_f123) in  [Lesson 8.5 - Reuse Game Logic](#part0013_split_001.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f9db5b5b34423341_f01b).logical AND operatorThe logical AND operator, &&, is used to determine whether two tests both evaluate to true. If the test on the left side is false, Java does not perform the test on the right side.See Key Points and More in Lesson 5.1 - If Statements, Strings that are Equal or Contain Letters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.logical OR operatorThe logical OR operator, ||, is used to determine whether at least one of two tests evaluates to true. If the test on the left side is true, Java does not perform the test on the right side.See Key Points and More in Lesson 5.1 - If Statements, Strings that are Equal or Contain Letters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.longA long is a basic data type in Java. A long [variable](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1efec72ee65afe7_1105b) can hold an [integer](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d0ddb62fa6bbd7f5_100e3) value between -9,223,372,036,854,775,808 and 9,223,372,036,854,775,807. To specify a long value in a program, type the value without quotation marks.See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Integer Data Type and Addition in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.look and feelThe look and feel of a system refers to how an operating system displays [components](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685) and how the components work on that operating system (for example Windows, OS X, or Linux). Most often, a Java programmer will set a program to use either the system look and feel or the cross-platform look and feel. Using the system look and feel, a program's display appearance and behavior may vary when run on each operating system. Using the cross-platform look and feel, the program's display appearance and behavior will be the same when run on any operating system, but may not match the display appearance or behavior of other types of programs run on a particular operating system.See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.10 - Cross Platform Look and Feel in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.main() methodThe main() method is the first [method](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c) [called](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e67f7ce0908d82ce_f4f2) when a program starts.See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Classes, Superclasses and Programs in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.maximizedWhen a [window](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_185c8a7e93daf2eb_1110e) is maximized, it fills the entire display area of the computer's monitor or screen.See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.6 - Window Size and Position in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.menuA menu is a drop down list of one or more choices, called [menu items](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_b7f6aa8fa05e49db_1060b), on a [menu bar](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_6bd486b000c0e5bf_105f4). Use [JMenu](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_3b983cd7595f733a_10272) to create a menu.See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Menu Bars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.menu barA menu bar is a row of one or more [menus](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_effccf0fec923ae6_105dd), usually stretched across the top of a [container](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_b473cd3a3256c48c_f7a9). Use [JMenuBar](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_5927a022bc23803a_10286) to create a menu bar.See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Menu Bars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.menu itemA menu item is a [clickable](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_6414c477fad92f99_f5d8) choice in a [menu](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_effccf0fec923ae6_105dd). When the menu item is clicked, an [ActionEvent](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_963da834c79f1fe9_f20b) is sent. If the program is [listening](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_bd0561f4b8c8108a_1049e) for the [event](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_3922a8ab0211a33d_fa62), the program will usually respond in some way. Use [JMenuItem](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_2440d6b4f48eccec_1029a) to create a menu item.See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Menu Bars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.message dialogA message dialog is a [dialog](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d50e18f9bae39dff_f933) whose purpose is simply to display a message.See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.8 - Message Dialogs in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.methodA method is a named [block of code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_87fccad38ae0c449_f36e) that can be [called](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e67f7ce0908d82ce_f4f2) from within the program.See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.3 - Methods in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.1 - Methods with Parameters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.3 - Methods that Return a Value in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Static Methods in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.3 - Methods with Multiple Parameters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.minimizedWhen a [window](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_185c8a7e93daf2eb_1110e) is minimized, it is removed from the screen but the program that displayed it is still running and accessible. In Microsoft Windows, a minimized window is displayed as an icon in the [task bar](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d072c574fb2fe807_10e70). Clicking on the window's icon in the [task bar](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d072c574fb2fe807_10e70) will return the [window](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_185c8a7e93daf2eb_1110e) to the display, at the window's previous location, and having its previous size.See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.6 - Window Size and Position in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.modalA [dialog](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d50e18f9bae39dff_f933) may be modal or [non-modal](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_c172062a1c470f3a_10833). When a modal dialog is displayed, the program stops to wait for the [user](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f7ee8b295ae825fc_1104a) to close the dialog. Use a modal dialog if the program should wait for user input before proceeding.See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.3 - Get Dialog Data in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.modelIn a [model/view/controller](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_4df0674422c946cc_106c8) design approach, the model holds the domain [objects](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_71c0aa408ef2c4da_10871) and the [logic](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e7cc05551c45ca60_1054f) that define how the objects interact in the domain.See [Key Points and More](#part0013_split_001.xhtml_anchor-0_1_34f7d8274f6c8efc_efc9) in [Lesson 8.4 - Set up Game Logic in the “Model”](#part0013_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_9090668e52edb67e_ce59).See [Key Points and More](#part0013_split_001.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d81848ff966b0cc6_f123) in [Lesson 8.5 - Reuse Game Logic](#part0013_split_001.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f9db5b5b34423341_f01b).model/view/controllerModel/View/Controller design organizes [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f) into three separate categories: The [model](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_bca0387e5a348c25_106a4) holds the domain [objects](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_71c0aa408ef2c4da_10871) and [logic](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e7cc05551c45ca60_1054f) that define how the objects interact in the domain. The [view](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_9625e49bae9e0ad0_11070) presents the program's information to the [user](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f7ee8b295ae825fc_1104a) and allows user input into the program. The [controller](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c3c33d34cfa62c1_f7cd) interprets the domain object data and controls the flow of information between the model and the view.See [Key Points and More](#part0013_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_160b913137435593_c2e1) in [Lesson 8.1 - Lay out the Display in the “View”](#part0013_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_472610cf486ab292_b7e0).See [Key Points and More](#part0013_split_001.xhtml_anchor-0_1_34f7d8274f6c8efc_efc9) in [Lesson 8.4 - Set up Game Logic in the “Model”](#part0013_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_9090668e52edb67e_ce59).See [Key Points and More](#part0013_split_001.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d81848ff966b0cc6_f123) in [Lesson 8.5 - Reuse Game Logic](#part0013_split_001.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f9db5b5b34423341_f01b).moduloModulo is the remainder after dividing two numbers.See Key Points and More in Lesson 16.3 - Modulo in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.mouse listenerA mouse listeners is a [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) that [extends](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1257f907c91f465_fb7e) the [MouseListener](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_6b130b8c6b00e752_107c0) class. A mouse listener waits for [MouseEvents](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_fa423773cb80b41f_10789).See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.1 - Mouse Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See [Key Points and More](#part0007.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d64e258bf6fb17c6_2f82) in [Lesson 2.1 - Drag Objects, Use a Dictionary](#part0007.xhtml_anchor-0_1_de184c329bfa417a_12ab).mouse motion listenerA mouse motion listener is a [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) that [extends](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1257f907c91f465_fb7e) the [MouseMotionListener](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_c2a7212c83f9a3a_1080b) class. A mouse listener waits for [MouseEvents](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_fa423773cb80b41f_10789).See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Draw with a Mouse, Mouse Motion Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See [Key Points and More](#part0007.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d64e258bf6fb17c6_2f82) in [Lesson 2.1 - Drag Objects, Use a Dictionary](#part0007.xhtml_anchor-0_1_de184c329bfa417a_12ab).MouseAdapterA MouseAdapter is a [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) that eases [MouseListener](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_6b130b8c6b00e752_107c0) [object](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_71c0aa408ef2c4da_10871) creation. Using a MouseAdapter, a programmer writes [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f) only for the MouseListener's [methods](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c) that will be used, rather than having to write code for all the methods [defined](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1222d6b11f73bdf2_f8f2) in MouseListener. A MouseAdapter may be used wherever a MouseListener is required.See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.1 - Mouse Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Draw with a Mouse, Mouse Motion Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See [Key Points and More](#part0007.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d64e258bf6fb17c6_2f82) in [Lesson 2.1 - Drag Objects, Use a Dictionary](#part0007.xhtml_anchor-0_1_de184c329bfa417a_12ab).MouseEventA MouseEvent is an [event](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_3922a8ab0211a33d_fa62) caused by a program [user](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f7ee8b295ae825fc_1104a) clicking a mouse [button](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a7e3bb01f1245fef_f441). Add a [MouseListener](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_6b130b8c6b00e752_107c0) or a [MouseMotionListener](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_c2a7212c83f9a3a_1080b) to a [component](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685) to [run](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_33acc39cc7b992b0_10ba9) [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f) when a MouseEvent occurs.See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.1 - Mouse Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Draw with a Mouse, Mouse Motion Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See [Key Points and More](#part0007.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d64e258bf6fb17c6_2f82) in [Lesson 2.1 - Drag Objects, Use a Dictionary](#part0007.xhtml_anchor-0_1_de184c329bfa417a_12ab).MouseListenerA MouseListener waits for a [MouseEvent](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_fa423773cb80b41f_10789) from its assigned [component](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685). When a MouseEvent occurs, Java [calls](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e67f7ce0908d82ce_f4f2) the MouseListener's mouseClicked(), mouseEntered(), mouseExited(), mousePressed(), or mouseReleased() [method](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c).See Key Points and More in Lesson 9.1 - Mouse Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Draw with a Mouse, Mouse Motion Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.MouseMotionAdapterA MouseMotionAdapter is a [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) that eases [MouseMotionListener](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_c2a7212c83f9a3a_1080b) [object](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_71c0aa408ef2c4da_10871) creation. Using a MouseMotionAdapter, a programmer writes [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f) only for the MouseMotionListener's [methods](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c) that will be used, rather than having to write code for all the methods [defined](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1222d6b11f73bdf2_f8f2) in MouseMotionListener. A MouseMotionAdapter may be used wherever a MouseMotionListener is required.See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Draw with a Mouse, Mouse Motion Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.MouseMotionListenerA MouseMotionListener waits for a [MouseEvent](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_fa423773cb80b41f_10789) from its assigned [component](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685). When a MouseEvent occurs, Java [calls](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e67f7ce0908d82ce_f4f2) the MouseMotionListener's mouseDragged() or mouseMoved() [method](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c).See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Draw with a Mouse, Mouse Motion Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.non-character dataCharacter data is data made up of characters that can be inserted into [strings](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_636f36eeb6f3b8f0_10d22). Non-character data is data made up of bit-patterns, such as image file data, that cannot be inserted into strings.non-modalA [dialog](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d50e18f9bae39dff_f933) may be [modal](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_578d862988f2efbe_1068d) or non-modal. When a non-modal dialog is displayed, the program continues to [run](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_33acc39cc7b992b0_10ba9). Use a non-modal dialog if the dialog should remain displayed while the program [user](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f7ee8b295ae825fc_1104a) continues interacting with the rest of the program.See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.3 - Get Dialog Data in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.not operatorThe not operator, !, inverts the value of a boolean or returns the complement of a test evaluation. For example, !true returns false.See Key Points and More in Lesson 5.1 - If Statements, Strings that are Equal or Contain Letters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.NumberFormatExceptionA NumberFormatException is an [exception](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_5826432d39c38488_fb22) [thrown](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7af6f0b4fdec3e27_10f0a) if a program cannot successfully convert a value to a number. For example, if a program tries to convert “abc” to a number, that program will throw a NumberFormatException.See Lesson 8.4 - Try/Catch Blocks and Exceptions in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.objectAn object is an [instance](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e84a0124fd42c25e_1008f) of a [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592). The object holds the information [defined](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1222d6b11f73bdf2_f8f2) in the class and can be operated on by the class's [methods](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c).See Key Points and More in Lesson 16.1 - Objects, Card in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.ObjectA Java class named Object is the base class of all Java classes.See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.3 - Event Source in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.overrideConsider overriding a [method](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c) whenever a [superclass](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f2efb435a19e5114_10da2) provides a method that you want to operate differently in a class you define. To override a method, create a method in your class, with the exact same name, [static](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_9407a2e934506325_10cee) modifier, [return](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e35d24884a00e0a6_10b1a) [type](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_883d6ce41c13bb5f_10ff1), and [parameters](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_17ebea10ad901503_1092e) as the [method](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c) defined(define) in the superclass. The visibility of your method need not be identical to, but cannot be more [visible](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_84bece005f8318cf_1109e), than the method it overrides.See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.2 - Key Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See [Key Points and More](#part0006.xhtml_anchor-0_1_cd7c113563a5eb33_79d) in [Lesson 1.2 - Create a Standard Custom Panel](#part0006.xhtml_anchor-0_1_b52c459dd49d1c3d_679).See [Key Points and More](#part0007.xhtml_anchor-0_1_97160553c4222148_31a8) in [Lesson 2.2 - Integrate the Timer](#part0007.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e22d3150035499a0_3000).packPacking a [window](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_185c8a7e93daf2eb_1110e) tells Java to resize the window and arrange all of its [components](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685) in the smallest possible area, considering all the components' [layouts](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_c1ec2d706f09968d_10446) and [preferred sizes](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e9343816b6879acf_1099e).See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.5 - Pack a Window in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.packagePackages contain one or more [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) files that are typically used together.See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.1 - Java Projects and Packages in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See [Create a First Package](#part0018.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1f8fab0afc375bfb_145a4) in [Appendix D - Using Eclipse](#part0018.xhtml).panelA panel is a [container](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_b473cd3a3256c48c_f7a9) that can hold many [components](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685), including other panels. Use [JPanel](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7741c4fb7a632007_102cc) to create panels.See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.2 - Panels, Predefined Colors in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.3 - Multiple Panels, Preferred Size, Dimension in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.Panels are also often used as drawing surfaces for program-created [objects](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_71c0aa408ef2c4da_10871) for which Java has no components, such as dice, letter tiles, and cards.See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.1 - A Painted Panel: Color, Rectangles, lines, Circles, and Preferred Size in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.parameter[Methods](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c) are [defined](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1222d6b11f73bdf2_f8f2) to expect zero or more input values, referred to as [arguments](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_99a431298dd48907_f2bd). These expected input values are [declared](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_8f52562663593280_f878) in the [method](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c) as parameters, each with a [variable](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1efec72ee65afe7_1105b) [type](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_883d6ce41c13bb5f_10ff1) and name. The method then uses those variables to access the value of the argument [passed](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_837e620690c2ef56_1095e) to the method when the method is [called](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e67f7ce0908d82ce_f4f2).See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.1 - Methods with Parameters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.3 - Methods with Multiple Parameters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.passPassing a value to a [method](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c) with [defined](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1222d6b11f73bdf2_f8f2) [parameters](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_17ebea10ad901503_1092e) means the program sends the value to the method as an [argument](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_99a431298dd48907_f2bd), when the method is [called](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e67f7ce0908d82ce_f4f2).See Lesson 7.1 - Methods with Parameters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.PNGPNG is a format for image files. “PNG” stands for Portable Network Graphics. A PNG file is usually named with “.png” as its extension.See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.1 - Transparent Colors, PNG Images in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.PointA Point is a [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) that holds two [integers](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d0ddb62fa6bbd7f5_100e3), usually representing x and y [coordinates](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_cbaf9bb1aae1460d_f803).See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.6 - Window Size and Position in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.preferred sizeA [component's](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685) preferred size consists of a programmer's desired width and height values (a [Dimension](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_c96e707926bc085b_f963)) for the component. Some [layouts](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_c1ec2d706f09968d_10446) display components at their preferred size, others do not.See Key Points and More in Lesson 2.3 - Multiple Panels, Preferred Size, Dimension in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.Always provide the preferred size of a [panel](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_3b846c32aa26cc4f_10905) that holds no components, such as a panel used as a drawing surface, by overriding the panel's getPreferredSize() method. Otherwise that panel might have no reserved space in the [layout](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_c1ec2d706f09968d_10446).See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.1 - A Painted Panel: Color, Rectangles, Lines, Circles, and Preferred Size in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.primitiveThe Java primitive data [types](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_883d6ce41c13bb5f_10ff1) are [int](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_92b7614274f15d5e_100cf), [double](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_c1e18040e6f72b93_f98c), [char](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f60e798719fa52c1_f57b), [boolean](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_16e20a7387b40372_f37f), [byte](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_fe763560a9de37c_f4de), [short](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f2111e4ae8f7461f_10c19), [long](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_9e655349e5fdc8e3_1058a), and [float](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d9b7d8aba5a9a0c6_fc78). The primitive types require no [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) [definitions](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1222d6b11f73bdf2_f8f2), and are manipulated using language-defined operations, rather than by [calling](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e67f7ce0908d82ce_f4f2) [methods.](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c)See Key Points and More in Lesson 15.5 - Array Lists in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.privateA [variable](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1efec72ee65afe7_1105b) or [method](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c) [declared](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_8f52562663593280_f878) as private can only be used in the declaring [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592).See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.3 - Methods in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.7 - Extend the DIYWindow Class in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Static Methods in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 14.3 - Instance Variables in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.protectedA protected [variable](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1efec72ee65afe7_1105b) or [method](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c) is normally only used within its own class or subclass. However, it may also be accessed by an object created from its class's class or subclass as long as the object is created in the same package.See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.7 - Extend the DIYWindow Class in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.publicA [variable](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1efec72ee65afe7_1105b) or [method](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c) [declared](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_8f52562663593280_f878) as public can be accessed by an [object](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_71c0aa408ef2c4da_10871) created from its class's class or subclass, in any [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) in the same [build path](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_16ade889aa555e58_f423).See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.7 - Extend the DIYWindow Class in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Static Methods in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 14.3 - Instance Variables in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.Quick FixThe Quick Fix feature of Eclipse lists ways Eclipse thinks a [syntax error](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_eefe20bb92c9c34a_10e59) could be fixed. To use Quick Fix, rest your mouse on the underlined error in the [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f). Eclipse will list ways to fix the problem. Select one of the options and Eclipse will fix the error for you.See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Classes, Superclasses and Programs in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.radio buttonA radio button is a [clickable](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_6414c477fad92f99_f5d8) [component](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685) with text. A radio button has only two states: selected or not selected. Use [JRadioButton](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_18236a8dbe595115_102f5) to create radio buttons. Radio buttons are usually added to a [button group](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_4bb308ced4b26edc_f4aa), in which only one radio button may be selected at a time. Use [ButtonGroup](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_79f984d021e78dc2_f4c7) to create button groups.See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.2 - Text Fields, Radio Buttons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.repaintWhen a program repaints a [component](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685), the program asks Java to draw the entire component again. A component should be repainted whenever the program changes [variable](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1efec72ee65afe7_1105b) values that might affect how the component should look. Use the component's repaint() method to repaint the component. The program should [revalidate](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_343d27f0427d700f_10b3a) instead of repaint the component after adding or removing objects displayed on the component.See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.1 - A Painted Panel: Color, Rectangles, Lines, Circles, and Preferred Size in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See [Key Points and More](#part0009.xhtml_anchor-0_1_3a7ec12ed85062a8_5f94) in [Lesson 4.3 - Reduce Animation Flicker](#part0009.xhtml_anchor-0_1_c1a7902c6c4170b3_5c8e).See [Key Points and More](#part0013_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_591f5ef148bde4bb_c886) in [Lesson 8.2 - Stop All Activity with a Sleeping Thread](#part0013_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_83ab6d7df4fe020_c2f6).resolvedGetting a [syntax error](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_eefe20bb92c9c34a_10e59) that a [variable](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1efec72ee65afe7_1105b) name cannot be resolved means the variable is not yet [defined](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1222d6b11f73bdf2_f8f2). This error may be fixed by [declaring](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_8f52562663593280_f878) the variable either as an instance or static variable or as a local variable in the method before the [variable](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1efec72ee65afe7_1105b) is used.See Lesson 7.1 - Methods with Parameters in Do-It-Yourself Java GamesGetting a [syntax error](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_eefe20bb92c9c34a_10e59) that a [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) name cannot be resolved means the class is not yet [defined](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1222d6b11f73bdf2_f8f2) or not accessible. This error is usually fixed by using [Quick Fix](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_53a2845c480e6047_10a6b) to [import](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_c3e10909de23d057_ff85) the needed class. If Quick Fix does not list the class, you may need to add the class's [library](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_3a080fa209b60d54_10483) or [Java project](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_cf63a8be27d3ec24_101b3) to the [build path](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_16ade889aa555e58_f423) for the current Java project.See Lesson 9.2 - Generate Random Numbers in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.resourceA program's resources include any additional files that are needed to allow the program to [run](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_33acc39cc7b992b0_10ba9). The resources often include data files and image files.See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.7 - Put Data Files in the JAR File in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.returnA [method](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c) may optionally return a value. One ore more return statements can be coded in a method. Whenever a return statement is run, control flow returns to the code that called the method. If a method returns a value, the [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f) that [called](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e67f7ce0908d82ce_f4f2) the method may assign the results of that [call](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e67f7ce0908d82ce_f4f2) to a [variable](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1efec72ee65afe7_1105b) of the same [type](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_883d6ce41c13bb5f_10ff1) as the returned value.See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.3 - Methods that Return a Value in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.revalidateWhen a program revalidates a [component](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685), the program is asking Java to again perform the [layout](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_c1ec2d706f09968d_10446) of that component and any contained components. A program should revalidate a component when the program adds, removes, or resizes any component object within that component.See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.3 - Add and Remove Components in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.1 - A Painted Panel: Color, Rectangles, Lines, Circles, and Preferred Size in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.rigid componentRigid components are often added to a [BoxLayout](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_6eecab2ef493de1c_f3a4) to add space between [components](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685). Rigid components are invisible, but will take up the exact amount of space [defined](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1222d6b11f73bdf2_f8f2) for them. Use a [glue component](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_6f43554da265537b_fdcf) instead if an invisible component is needed that should stretch to fill remaining space.See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.3 - Space Between Components in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.root paneA [JFrame](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a2e632130691a36_10227) [window](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_185c8a7e93daf2eb_1110e) is actually made up of several panes, one of which is the root pane. Explanation of all these panes is beyond the scope of this book. However, you need to know that to use a button as a [default button](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_ffbb4c96203c079b_f8be), a program must get the [JFrame](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a2e632130691a36_10227) [object's](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_71c0aa408ef2c4da_10871) root pane, and set its [default button](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_ffbb4c96203c079b_f8be).See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.6 - A Default Button in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.row-major orderJava [arrays](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_59e210b3f891158a_f2f3) are stored in row-major order. Row-major order means data is stored for the first dimension first, followed by the second, etc. If an array is [defined](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1222d6b11f73bdf2_f8f2) as having two [dimensions](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_c96e707926bc085b_f963), row and column, with row being its first dimension, Java would store all the data for row 1, then the data for row 2, etc.See [Key Points and More](#part0010.xhtml_anchor-0_1_58ddebf56fb69f6f_6a12) in [Lesson 5.1 - Use a Multi-Dimensional Array](#part0010.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a0b69e76a526902d_5ff0).runWhen a program is run, Java [calls](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e67f7ce0908d82ce_f4f2) the program's [main()](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e7e1b0c0266556af_105af) [method](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e7e1b0c0266556af_105af) and runs the instructions of each line of [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f) in sequence.See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Classes, Superclasses and Programs in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.RunnableRunnable is an [interface](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d74c9b6cbdca9d02_10111) whose only [method](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c) is run().See [Key Points and More](#part0006.xhtml_anchor-0_1_cca9f924d165cb5_b87) in [Lesson 1.5 - Create a Thread](#part0006.xhtml_anchor-0_1_8d852bced73c109_afb).See [Key Points and More](#part0008.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7130df9394b0c4e2_49a2) in [Lesson 3.3 - Define a Thread Inline](#part0008.xhtml_anchor-0_1_639dcd699dd1c581_419c).scroll barsScroll bars are slider [components](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685) that are added to the side and/or bottom of another component 's display if that other component does not fit in its [container](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_b473cd3a3256c48c_f7a9). Sliders allow a program [user](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f7ee8b295ae825fc_1104a) to scroll through the parts of the component that did not fit on the display. To easily add scroll bars to a component, put it in a [JScrollPane](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_2a7073cb45fb2845_10309).See Key Points and More in Lesson 3.2 - Scroll Bars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.serial version UIDThe serial version UID is meant to be a unique ID assigned to the current version of a [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592). The serial version UID is only used if its [defining](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1222d6b11f73bdf2_f8f2) class is serialized. None of the classes in this book will be serialized, and serialization is beyond the scope of this book. You may ignore the warning Eclipse gives about the missing serialVersionUID given when you [extend](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1257f907c91f465_fb7e) one of the Java [Swing](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_de31657f4ed0ea83_10ddf) classes.See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.8 - Serial Version UID in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.shortShort is a basic data [type](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_883d6ce41c13bb5f_10ff1) in Java. A short [variable](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1efec72ee65afe7_1105b) can hold an [integer](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d0ddb62fa6bbd7f5_100e3) value between -32,768 and 32,767\. To specify a short value in a program, type the value without quotation marks.See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.1 - Integer Data Type and Addition in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.SimpleDateFormatSimpleDateFormat is a [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) that [defines](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1222d6b11f73bdf2_f8f2) how a [Date](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_994a7c06c504d776_f841) is to be displayed as a [string](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_636f36eeb6f3b8f0_10d22). For example, a SimpleDateFormat may include month names or month numbers, it may include the time or only the day, and it may include extra characters: comma, slash, dash, colon, or others.See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.4 - Current Date, Date Format in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.sourceMany [events](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_3922a8ab0211a33d_fa62) define a [method](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c) for getting the source of the event. Getting the source will [return](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e35d24884a00e0a6_10b1a) the [component](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685) on which the event occurred.See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.3 - Event Source in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.stack traceA stack trace may be used to get more information about an exception that is thrown. A printed stack trace consists of the [exception's](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_5826432d39c38488_fb22) message, followed by a list of the [method](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c) [calls](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e67f7ce0908d82ce_f4f2) and the [classes](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) from which they were called, that preceded the exception. Use Exception's printStackTrace() method to print a stack trace to the [console](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a35c40908fadebe8_f777).See [Key Points and More](#part0012_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_38ab58201d404b72_9cb7) in [Lesson 7.2 - Create and Throw Custom Exceptions](#part0012_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_56f1af00984edb6c_94c3).state-driven programmingState-driven programming is designing code to control program activity based on the [defined](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1222d6b11f73bdf2_f8f2) possible states of an object or program. The program determines which [methods](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c) to [call](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e67f7ce0908d82ce_f4f2) based on the current state's value. The methods then change the state's value as appropriate. State-driven code may be written using a switch block or [if statements](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d4c8c577a58feec1_fe80), or it may be written using state [objects](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_71c0aa408ef2c4da_10871) whose [classes](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) [implement](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_5f1e072a6ae679dc_ff4b) a state [interface](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d74c9b6cbdca9d02_10111).See [Key Points and More](#part0011.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1966537877e75b08_8f48) in [Lesson 6.1 - Use State-Driven Programming, Detect Collisions of Non-Rectangular Shapes](#part0011.xhtml_anchor-0_1_fa53d8bf72346ee2_7827).See [Key Points and More](#part0012_split_001.xhtml_anchor-0_1_3abf22024cff18fa_b75f) in [Lesson 7.4 - Use an Interface for State-Driven Design](#part0012_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_3f8e0064ae101500_a024).statementA statement is a complete line of [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f), usually up to and including the ending semicolon. Some statements, such as [if statements](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d4c8c577a58feec1_fe80) and [switch statements](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_c6fddee256a7d5b_10e2a), include a [block of code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_87fccad38ae0c449_f36e). Such statements end after the block of code instead of after a semicolon.See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Classes, Superclasses and Programs in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 5.1 - If Statements, Strings that are Equal or Contain Letters in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.2 - Switch Statements in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.2 - While Loops in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.1 - For Loops in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.staticStatic [methods](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c) are self-contained. They can only use their parameter values and static variables; they cannot use the [class's](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) [instance variables](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_8e59a25ee8ca9e_100a9). A static method may be [called](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e67f7ce0908d82ce_f4f2) by using its class name followed by the method name.See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Static Methods in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.Static [variables](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1efec72ee65afe7_1105b) are shared by every [object](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_71c0aa408ef2c4da_10871) created from the class. If one object updates the value of a static variable, all objects created from that class see the same new value for that variable. Static variables must be [declared](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_8f52562663593280_f878) in a [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) [definition](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1222d6b11f73bdf2_f8f2), not in a [method](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c).See Key Points and More in Lesson 14.6 - Static Final Variables in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.stringA string is text with zero or more characters of any kind. String [variables](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1efec72ee65afe7_1105b) are [declared](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_8f52562663593280_f878) in Java as “String”. To specify a string value in a program, type the text surrounded with double quotation marks.See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.3 - Variables, Strings, and the Escape Character in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.2 - Convert a String to an Integer in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.1 - Order of Operation in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.2 - String Length and Substring in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.4 - Index of Characters in a String in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 14.2 - Replace Characters in a String in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.stubStub [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f) is an automatically-generated [method](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c) [declaration](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_8f52562663593280_f878). The content of the method is left empty for the programmer to write himself.See [Create a First Program](#part0018.xhtml_anchor-0_1_eea89fcb904b339e_145ff) in [Appendix D - Using Eclipse](#part0018.xhtml).subimageA subimage is a rectangular portion of an image.See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.2 - Read Image Files, Subimages, Image Icons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.super()Use super() as the first line of [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f) in a [method](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c) to [call](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e67f7ce0908d82ce_f4f2) that method in the [class's](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) [superclass](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f2efb435a19e5114_10da2).See [Key Points and More](#part0007.xhtml_anchor-0_1_97160553c4222148_31a8) in [Lesson 2.2 - Integrate the Timer](#part0007.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e22d3150035499a0_3000).superclassA superclass is a [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) from which the current class is derived. All classes without a [defined](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1222d6b11f73bdf2_f8f2) superclass have Object as their superclass. Any class may be used as a superclass. An [object](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_71c0aa408ef2c4da_10871) created from a class is considered to be “a kind of” its superclass, and may use any of the [public](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_2b5021a090ed4135_10a3d) or [protected](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e15aad0bd742db76_10a29) [variables](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1efec72ee65afe7_1105b) or [methods](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c) of its superclass. For example, a class which names DIYWindow as its superclass is a kind of DIYWindow and may use the print() and input() methods defined by DIYWindow.See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Classes, Superclasses and Programs in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.7 - Extend the DIYWindow Class in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See [Create a First Program](#part0018.xhtml_anchor-0_1_eea89fcb904b339e_145ff) in [Appendix D - Using Eclipse](#part0018.xhtml).SwingJava Swing is the collection of [user](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f7ee8b295ae825fc_1104a) interface [components](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685) in the javax [package](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_933bf66eb34c8a11_108eb). Swing component names all start with a J, such as [JFrame](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a2e632130691a36_10227), [JPanel](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7741c4fb7a632007_102cc), and [JButton](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a51ccb175c0ff638_101d6).See [Key Points and More](#part0006.xhtml_anchor-0_1_578505eb0f9d4203_629) in [Lesson 1.1 - Create a Standard Project and Class](#part0006.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a3719cd6f765c4e7_4bd).See [Key Points and More](#part0009.xhtml_anchor-0_1_264d122e067c8a08_518b) in [Lesson 4.1 - Animate with a Swing Timer](#part0009.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f51d08ef483d998a_4a22).See [Key Points and More](#part0009.xhtml_anchor-0_1_3a7ec12ed85062a8_5f94) in [Lesson 4.3 - Reduce Animation Flicker](#part0009.xhtml_anchor-0_1_c1a7902c6c4170b3_5c8e).See [Key Points and More](#part0013_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_160b913137435593_c2e1) in [Lesson 8.1 - Lay out the Display in the “View”](#part0013_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_472610cf486ab292_b7e0).See [Key Points and More](#part0013_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_591f5ef148bde4bb_c886) in [Lesson 8.2 - Stop All Activity with a Sleeping Thread](#part0013_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_83ab6d7df4fe020_c2f6).switch statementA switch statement is a [block of code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_87fccad38ae0c449_f36e) that [runs](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_33acc39cc7b992b0_10ba9) different [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f) for each expected value of a [variable](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1efec72ee65afe7_1105b).See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.2 - Switch Statements in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.4 - Switch Default in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 13.6 - Case without Break in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 15.1 - Switch Statement with Integers in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.syntax errorA syntax error occurs if [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f) does not meet the order or content rules required by Java. All syntax errors must be fixed before a program can [run](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_33acc39cc7b992b0_10ba9). Eclipse provides a [Quick Fix](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_53a2845c480e6047_10a6b) tool to easily fix syntax errors.See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Classes, Superclasses and Programs in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.task barMicrosoft Windows has a task bar, usually displayed across the bottom of the screen, that contains an icon for each program that currently displays a window. Clicking any of the icons in the task bar brings the selected window to the front of the other windows.See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.7 - Window Title, Center in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.text fieldA text field is a [component](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685) that allows a program [user](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f7ee8b295ae825fc_1104a) to enter one line of character data to be used as input to the program. Create a text field using [JTextField](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_47930b4d525690a3_10334).See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.2 - Text Fields, Radio Buttons in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.3 - Focus Listeners in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.threadA thread is a mechanism that allows each line of [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f) assigned to the thread to [run](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_33acc39cc7b992b0_10ba9) one line at a time along its designed code path. Multiple threads allows multiple code paths to run at the same time, one code path per thread. Every program runs in a main thread. Every program that uses [Swing](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_de31657f4ed0ea83_10ddf) functionality runs a main thread and its Swing operations run in an [event dispatch thread](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_812588057eecf796_faa6). Audio is played in yet another thread. There are many ways to create additional threads. This book creates addition threads using the Thread class or the Swing Timer class.Thread is the Java [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) used to create a new thread.See [Key Points and More](#part0006.xhtml_anchor-0_1_2c1a8da17a780d1d_ad0) in [Lesson 1.4 - Pause a Thread](#part0006.xhtml_anchor-0_1_19dfa28a2993c391_936).See [Key Points and More](#part0006.xhtml_anchor-0_1_cca9f924d165cb5_b87) in [Lesson 1.5 - Create a Thread](#part0006.xhtml_anchor-0_1_8d852bced73c109_afb).See [Key Points and More](#part0006.xhtml_anchor-0_1_b217ba14343b6cb3_f9b) in [Lesson 1.6 - Stop a Thread](#part0006.xhtml_anchor-0_1_4d6fc544802f1a5a_c23).See [Key Points and More](#part0008.xhtml_anchor-0_1_61614548c2a13f76_4152) in [Lesson 3.2 - Pause the Event Dispatch Thread](#part0008.xhtml_anchor-0_1_71c56116e9af500_3bb4).See [Key Points and More](#part0008.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7130df9394b0c4e2_49a2) in [Lesson 3.3 - Define a Thread Inline](#part0008.xhtml_anchor-0_1_639dcd699dd1c581_419c).See [Key Points and More](#part0009.xhtml_anchor-0_1_264d122e067c8a08_518b) in [Lesson 4.1 - Animate with a Swing Timer](#part0009.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f51d08ef483d998a_4a22).See [Key Points and More](#part0009.xhtml_anchor-0_1_3a7ec12ed85062a8_5f94) in [Lesson 4.3 - Reduce Animation Flicker](#part0009.xhtml_anchor-0_1_c1a7902c6c4170b3_5c8e).See [Key Points and More](#part0013_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_591f5ef148bde4bb_c886) in [Lesson 8.2 - Stop All Activity with a Sleeping Thread](#part0013_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_83ab6d7df4fe020_c2f6).throw an exceptionWhen a [running](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_33acc39cc7b992b0_10ba9) program encounters an [exception](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_5826432d39c38488_fb22), the program skips to the [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f) that [catches](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_c3929929bb8b579b_10fcd) that particular exception. If no [catch block](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_c3929929bb8b579b_10fcd) was written for that exception, the program terminates.See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.4 - Try/Catch Blocks and Exceptions in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See [Lesson 7.1 - Use System Exit Codes](#part0012_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_6c423710e7c6711e_8f99).See [Key Points and More](#part0012_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_38ab58201d404b72_9cb7) in [Lesson 7.2 - Create and Throw Custom Exceptions](#part0012_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_56f1af00984edb6c_94c3).TimerTimer is a [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) in the [Swing](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_de31657f4ed0ea83_10ddf) [package](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_933bf66eb34c8a11_108eb) whose start() [method](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c) will repeatedly [call](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e67f7ce0908d82ce_f4f2) its actionPerformed() method at set intervals. You must provide [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f) for the actionPerformed() method when you create a Timer. Timer [runs](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_33acc39cc7b992b0_10ba9) in a separate [thread](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_2a0963431d6e1d34_10ea3).See [Key Points and More](#part0009.xhtml_anchor-0_1_264d122e067c8a08_518b) in [Lesson 4.1 - Animate with a Swing Timer](#part0009.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f51d08ef483d998a_4a22).See [Key Points and More](#part0009.xhtml_anchor-0_1_3a7ec12ed85062a8_5f94) in [Lesson 4.3 - Reduce Animation Flicker](#part0009.xhtml_anchor-0_1_c1a7902c6c4170b3_5c8e).See [Key Points and More](#part0013_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_591f5ef148bde4bb_c886) in [Lesson 8.2 - Stop All Activity with a Sleeping Thread](#part0013_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_83ab6d7df4fe020_c2f6).titleSet the title of a program using [JFrame's](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a2e632130691a36_10227) setTitle() [method](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c).See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.7 - Window Title, Center in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.toolbarA toolbar is a row of [components](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685), typically displayed across the top of a [window](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_185c8a7e93daf2eb_1110e). Components in a toolbar are most often added as [image buttons](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_dc8e76d3f9ab4114_fec2), but may also include any other [types](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_883d6ce41c13bb5f_10ff1) of components. A [listener](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1544cc5956846959_104e5) should be programmed for each component in a toolbar, to perform an action when an [event](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_3922a8ab0211a33d_fa62) occurs on that component.See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.tool tipBecause [toolbar](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_313b277f9643eb_10f90) [components](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685) often display images instead of text, the corresponding tool's purpose might not always be obvious. Help the program [user](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f7ee8b295ae825fc_1104a) understand the tool's purpose by displaying a tool tip. A tool tip is the text displayed when the [user](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f7ee8b295ae825fc_1104a) rests his cursor on a tool image in the [toolbar](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_313b277f9643eb_10f90).See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.1 - Toolbars in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.try/catch blockA try/catch block consists of a try block and one or more catch blocks. Place [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f) that might [throw an exception](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7af6f0b4fdec3e27_10f0a) within a try block. Place code to be [run](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_33acc39cc7b992b0_10ba9) for each expected [exception](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_5826432d39c38488_fb22) in a catch block at the end of the try block. When an exception is thrown from within a try block, Java breaks out of the try block and runs the code in the corresponding catch block, before continuing with the code that follows the try/catch block. If there is no catch block for the thrown exception, Java breaks out of the current method and throws the exception to the code that called the method. If no calling method catches the exception, the program ends with a run-time error.See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.4 - Try/Catch Blocks and Exceptions in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.typeIn Java, the type of an [object](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_71c0aa408ef2c4da_10871) is defined by its [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) or its [superclass](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f2efb435a19e5114_10da2). For example, the HelloWorld class created in the first book is a type of DIYWindow; or a [variable](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1efec72ee65afe7_1105b) [declared](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_8f52562663593280_f878) as a [String](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_636f36eeb6f3b8f0_10d22) has String as its type.See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.2 - Classes, Superclasses and Programs in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.unhandled exceptionAn unhandled exception is an [exception](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_5826432d39c38488_fb22) for which no handling [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f) is provided. Add a [try/catch block](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_c3929929bb8b579b_10fcd) to handle exceptions. A program will stop with a run time error if the program runs into an unhandled exception.See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.4 - Try/Catch Blocks and Exceptions in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.unicodeUnicode provides a common representation of text characters that is meant to be independent of the device, program, or language that is working with the text. Unicode numbers have been assigned for all of the typable characters as well as for many symbols not found on a keyboard, such as hearts, diamonds, clubs, and spades.See Lesson 13.1 - Transparent Colors, PNG Images in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.unzipUnzip is the process of [extracting](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_3bee7fb4fedb657e_fb9e) files from a [ZIP file](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_ab33a1e023f7b50c_11235).See [Download and Install Eclipse](#part0017.xhtml_anchor-0_1_675f74414f058471_14479) in [Appendix C - Setup](#part0017.xhtml).userThe user is the person who is [running](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_33acc39cc7b992b0_10ba9) a program.See Key Points and More in Lesson 4.1 - Input a String in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.variableA variable is a named piece of data whose value can be changed.See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.3 - Variables, Strings, and the Escape Character in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 3.1 - Reuse Strings in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.viewIn a [model/view/controller](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_4df0674422c946cc_106c8) design approach, the view is the [user](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f7ee8b295ae825fc_1104a) interface. The view displays what happens in the [model](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_bca0387e5a348c25_106a4) and handles user interactions with the program.See [Key Points and More](#part0013_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_160b913137435593_c2e1) in [Lesson 8.1 - Lay out the Display in the “View”](#part0013_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_472610cf486ab292_b7e0).See [Key Points and More](#part0013_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_fea0f4dc45f45392_ce47) in [Lesson 8.3 - Define Listeners in a Different Class](#part0013_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7eda46bba6f2b51c_c8e5).See [Key Points and More](#part0013_split_001.xhtml_anchor-0_1_34f7d8274f6c8efc_efc9) in [Lesson 8.4 - Set up Game Logic in the “Model”](#part0013_split_000.xhtml_anchor-0_1_9090668e52edb67e_ce59).visibleIf a [variable](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1efec72ee65afe7_1105b) or [method](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c) is visible, it can be accessed by other [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f). The three different visibility settings are [private](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_fba82c792e60db22_109fa), [protected](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e15aad0bd742db76_10a29), and [public](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_2b5021a090ed4135_10a3d).See Key Points and More in Lesson 6.3 - Methods in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 8.7 - Extend the DIYWindow Class in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 12.5 - Static Methods in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 14.3 - Instance Variables in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.A [window](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_185c8a7e93daf2eb_1110e) or [dialog](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d50e18f9bae39dff_f933) must be made visible for it to be displayed. To make a window or dialog visible or invisible, use [JFrame's](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a2e632130691a36_10227) or [JDialog's](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7958542f2b56295f_101ff) setVisible() [method](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c). Instead of closing a dialog after the [user](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_f7ee8b295ae825fc_1104a) enters input, make the dialog not visible so the program can still access the data that the user entered.See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.1 - A Standard Window in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.1 - A Custom Dialog in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 10.3 - Get Dialog Data in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.while loopA while loop is a [block of code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_87fccad38ae0c449_f36e) that repeats while an expression evaluates to true.See Key Points and More in Lesson 7.2 - While Loops in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.windowA basic window consists of a large rectangular viewing area on a screen, usually having a [title](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_eabeb84ab4aecb76_10f7a) bar displayed across the top, and a border displayed around its edges. Many other [components](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685) can be added to a window. Use Java's [JFrame](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a2e632130691a36_10227) [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) to create a window.See Key Points and More in Lesson 1.1 - A Standard Window in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.window listenerA window listener is a [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) that [extends](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1257f907c91f465_fb7e) the [WindowListener](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7d6334250084eab2_111b2) [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592). A window listener waits for [WindowEvents](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_15772575b907e78a_11185).See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.6 - Window Size and Position in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.window state listenerA window state listener is a [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) that [extends](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a1257f907c91f465_fb7e) the [WindowStateListener](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_6aa3b7f85a1134df_111dd) [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592). A window state listener waits for [WindowEvents](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_15772575b907e78a_11185).See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.WindowAdapterWindowAdapter is a [class](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7f62e45a3f9d28c0_f592) that eases [WindowListener](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7d6334250084eab2_111b2) [object](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_71c0aa408ef2c4da_10871) creation. Using a WindowAdapter, a programmer must write [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f) only for the [WindowListener's](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7d6334250084eab2_111b2) [methods](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c) that will be used, rather than having to write code for all the methods [defined](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_1222d6b11f73bdf2_f8f2) in WindowListener. A WindowAdapter may be used wherever a WindowListener is required.See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.6 - Window Size and Position in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.WindowEventA WindowEvent is an [event](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_3922a8ab0211a33d_fa62) caused by a [window](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_185c8a7e93daf2eb_1110e) being: opened, closed, newly made active, made no longer active, [minimized](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_df3c309bf2882334_1066c), or returned to normal size. Add a [WindowListener](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7d6334250084eab2_111b2) or a [WindowStateListener](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_6aa3b7f85a1134df_111dd) to a [component](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685) to [run](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_33acc39cc7b992b0_10ba9) [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f) when the WindowEvent occurs.See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.6 - Window Size and Position in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.WindowListenerA WindowListener waits for a [WindowEvent](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_15772575b907e78a_11185) from its assigned [component](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685). When a [WindowEvent](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_15772575b907e78a_11185) occurs, Java [calls](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e67f7ce0908d82ce_f4f2) the WindowListener's windowActivated(), windowClosed(), windowClosing(), windowDeactivated(), windowDeiconified(), windowIconified(), or windowOpened() [method](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c).See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.6 - Window Size and Position in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.WindowStateListenerA WindowStateListener waits for a [WindowEvent](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_15772575b907e78a_11185) from its assigned [component](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_7c484cbc7975355_f685). When a [WindowEvent](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_15772575b907e78a_11185) occurs, Java [calls](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e67f7ce0908d82ce_f4f2) the WindowStateListener's windowStateChanged() [method](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_284287726093f58a_1063c).See Key Points and More in Lesson 11.5 - Component Listeners, Window State Listeners, Resize a Window in More Do-It-Yourself Java Games.work folderCreate a work folder to contain all the Java [code](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_e691006e9275e264_f60f) and other files needed for your programs.See [Create a Java Work Folder](#part0017.xhtml_anchor-0_1_709d8a33711c676e_14412) in [Appendix C - Setup](#part0017.xhtml).wrapperA wrapper exists for each of the Java [primitives](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a2edfb01eb7b5a61_109c5) and may be used to convert a Java [primitive](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_a2edfb01eb7b5a61_109c5) value into an [object](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_71c0aa408ef2c4da_10871). For example, Integer is a wrapper for [integers](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_d0ddb62fa6bbd7f5_100e3). You can create an Integer [object](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_71c0aa408ef2c4da_10871) called obj from an [int](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_92b7614274f15d5e_100cf) called num by using Integer obj = new Integer(num).See Key Points and More in Lesson 15.6 - Array Lists in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.ZIP fileA ZIP file contains the compressed contents of one or more folders or files. A ZIP file is named with “.zip” as its extension. Files must be [extracted](#part0015.xhtml_anchor-0_1_3bee7fb4fedb657e_fb9e) from a ZIP file before they can be used.See Download and Install Eclipse in Setup in Do-It-Yourself Java Games.See [Download and Install Eclipse](#part0017.xhtml_anchor-0_1_675f74414f058471_14479) in [Appendix C - Setup](#part0017.xhtml).Appendix B - Completed ListingsThese completed listings show what every listing in the book should look like after all changes have been made, blanks filled in, and code removed.Project 1 - My TimerListing 1-1, from MyTimer.java

  public void setTime(long time) {
    this.time = time;
    long h = time / 3600;
    long m = (time / 60) % 60;
    long s = time % 60;
    timeString = String.format("%02d:%02d:%02d", h, m, s);
    repaint();
  }

  public TimerPanel(long time, Font font) {
    setTime(time);
    setFont(font);

  public static ArrayList<String> readTextFile(Object requestor, String fileName) {
    ArrayList<String> lines = new ArrayList<String>();

    try {
      InputStream input = requestor.getClass().getResourceAsStream(fileName);
      BufferedReader in = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(input));
      String line = in.readLine();
      while (line != null) {
        lines.add(line);
        line = in.readLine();
      }
      in.close();
    }
    return lines;
  }

  public TileSet removeAndReturn1TileAt(int clickedX, int clickedY) {
    TileSet tileSet = null;
    for (int i = 0; i < tiles.size() && tileSet == null; i++) {
      int tileLeftEdge = x + (LetterTile.SIZE * i);
      int tileRightEdge = tileLeftEdge + LetterTile.SIZE;
      int tileTopEdge = y;
      int tileBottomEdge = y + LetterTile.SIZE;
      if (clickedX >= tileLeftEdge && clickedX <= tileRightEdge
          && clickedY >= tileTopEdge && clickedY <= tileBottomEdge) {
        LetterTile tile = tiles.get(i);
        String letter = tile.getLetter();
        tileSet = new TileSet(letter, tileLeftEdge, tileTopEdge);
        tiles.remove(i);
        if (i == 0) {
          x += LetterTile.SIZE;
        }
      }
    }
    return tileSet;
  }
    ...

  private void clicked(int x, int y, boolean leftClicked) {
    if (movingTiles == null) {
      mouseX = x;
      mouseY = y;

      for (int i = 0; i < tileSets.size() && movingTiles == null; i++) {
        TileSet tileSet = tileSets.get(i);
        if (tileSet.contains(x, y)) {
          if (leftClicked) {
            movingTiles = tileSet.removeAndReturn1TileAt(x, y);
            if (tileSet.getNumberOfTiles() == 0) {

  private void clicked(int x, int y) {
    int row = y / Cell.SIZE;
    int col = x / Cell.SIZE;

    int direction = getSwapDirection(x, y);

    switch(direction) {
    case DIRECTION_LEFT :
      swap(row, col, row, col - 1);
      break;
    case DIRECTION_RIGHT :
      swap(row, col, row, col + 1);
      break;
    case DIRECTION_UP :
      swap(row, col, row - 1, col);
      break;
    case DIRECTION_DOWN :
      swap(row, col, row + 1, col);
      break;  
    }
  }
    ...

  private int markChainsAndGetPointsInCol(int col) {
    int points = 0;

    // get the color of the first ball
    int color = cells[0][col].getColor();
    int count = 1;

    // loop through each row of the column
    for (int row = 1; row < ROWS; row++) {

      // count the balls in each color
      int nextColor = cells[row][col].getColor();
      if (nextColor == color) {
        count++;
      }
      else {
        color = nextColor;
        count = 1;
      }

      // mark chains of three or more. When count  
      // reaches 3, also mark previous two.
      if (count == 3) {
        cells[row][col].setInChain(true);
        cells[row - 1][col].setInChain(true);
        cells[row - 2][col].setInChain(true);
      }
      else if (count > 3) {
        cells[row][col].setInChain(true);
      }
    }

    return points;
  }

  private boolean validMovesRemaining() {
    boolean movesRemaining = false;
    for (int row = 0; row < ROWS && !movesRemaining; row++) {
      for (int col = 0; col < COLS && !movesRemaining; col++) {
        if (row < ROWS - 1) {
          movesRemaining = isValidSwap(row, col, DIRECTION_DOWN);
        }
        if (!movesRemaining && col < COLS - 1) {
          movesRemaining = isValidSwap(row, col, DIRECTION_RIGHT);

        }
      }
    }
    return movesRemaining;
  }

      String message = "No more birds remain. Do you want to play again?";
      int option = JOptionPane.showConfirmDialog(this, message,"Play again?", JOptionPane.YES_NO_OPTION);
      if (option == JOptionPane.YES_OPTION) {
        birdNestPanel.setBirdCount(LIVES - 1);
        scorePanel.reset();
        flightPanel.restart();
      }
      else {
        System.exit(0);
      }
    }
  }
